name: Adult Internal
description: Internal posting for adult services staff. The paper form scores 14 questions at 5 points each, 70% to pass.

questions.text: Do you have any conditions or previous injuries that might impact your ability to perform this role?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms whether they can perform the physical duties of the role, including transfers, lifting, personal care and Mandt physical interventions
- Identifies any accommodation they would need, and whether it can be discussed with the manager and follow up arranged
- Notes any restriction relevant to individual support duties, such as driving, overnight shifts or single staffed shifts
- Interviewer notes only what is needed for follow up; no medical detail or diagnosis is required at interview

questions.text: You and a co-worker are working a weekend shift together. How do you decide what to do for the day?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts from the person supported: their support plan, goals, routines, activity schedule and what they want to do that day
- Reads the communication book and logs from previous shifts for appointments, events, health notes or follow up
- Reviews shift duties and agrees with the co-worker who leads which activities, appointments and household tasks
- Stays flexible and trades off duties through the shift, checking in with each other as the day changes
- Problem solves together if the plan cannot be followed, and calls the manager for direction when needed
- Keeps the day driven by the person's choice rather than by staff preference or convenience

questions.text: What does a person-centered approach mean to you, and how have you applied it in your work?
questions.answerKey:
- The person supported is at the centre of planning and decisions about their own support
- Prioritises their goals, preferences, values and daily choices, including small everyday choices
- Builds on strengths and aspirations rather than focusing on deficits or compliance
- Supports self-determination and a more fulfilling life, including dignity of risk and community participation
- Gives a concrete example from their own work, including how they learned what mattered to the person and what changed as a result

questions.text: Please describe some ways that people who are non verbal may use to communicate. Please describe how you have supported someone who uses a communication system to communicate
questions.answerKey:
- Names a range of methods: pictures and symbols, objects, eye gaze, gestures, ASL, written words, iPad or device, vocalisations, and behaviour as communication
- Learned the person's system through orientation, reading their guidelines and watching experienced staff model it
- Uses the system consistently and gives the person time to respond rather than guessing or speaking for them
- Keeps the system available and portable, so it goes into the community and is used with others, not just in the home
- Models it for new and casual staff, raises how it is working at team meetings and documents in logs
- Gives a specific example of a person they supported and how communication improved or misunderstandings reduced

questions.text: What are individual support guidelines, and why are they important?
questions.answerKey:
- Documented direction on what is important to the person supported and what they want to accomplish
- Provide a framework for working toward personalised goals in a measurable way
- Written in modified, accessible language and format so the person can understand their own guidelines
- Include a staff action plan so everyone knows what they are responsible for
- Important because they keep support consistent across all staff and casuals and keep activities tied to the person's goals rather than staff habit

questions.text: What is an Individual Support Plan, and how do you use it in your role?
questions.answerKey:
- A service delivery plan built around the person's goals, with strategies that build on strengths and capacity
- Reflects the wants, needs, expectations and choices of the person supported
- Used daily to guide activities and supports, not read once and left in a binder
- Records activities, notes and progress regularly in ShareVision under the Individual Support Plan section
- Keeps all staff including casuals informed of current goals and who is responsible for what

questions.text: How are individual goals created, and how do you contribute to this process?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts with the person supported and their own stated interests and priorities
- Includes family and support network input where the person wants them involved
- Draws on quality of life domains and considers what is important to the person as well as important for them
- Staff contribute observations from daily support about what is working, emerging interests and realistic next steps
- Describes their own contribution: participating in planning discussions and team meetings, then supporting the goal consistently and documenting progress
- Goals are reviewed and adjusted as the person's interests or circumstances change

questions.text: What is a Safety Plan, and how is it implemented? (If applicable to the position/program)
questions.answerKey:
- An individualised written document setting out strategies and interventions to manage and reduce risks linked to challenging behaviour
- Directs staff on how to support the person when behaviour is critical or unsafe to themselves or others
- Written by a behavioural consultant (CBI) with input from the person supported, family and support network
- May contain restricted practices, which are used only as written and never improvised
- Staff are trained by the manager, and in some cases by the behavioural consultant, before implementing it
- Implemented consistently by all staff, with incidents documented and concerns about fit raised with the manager

questions.text: What types of reporting are you required to do as part of your job? Why is this reporting important?
questions.answerKey:
- Daily logs or contact notes and progress toward goals
- Personal charting such as body checks, bowel movements, seizures and weight charts
- Incident reporting (general, critical, reportable), medication records, overnight checks, vehicle pre-trip checks and mileage logs
- Explains why: keeps the whole team aware of what happened, meets CLBC and Licensing standards and health and safety requirements, tracks health and goal progress, and keeps support consistent for the person supported
- Vehicle damage scenario: document on the vehicle condition report with photos, notify the manager, check the pre-trip form to see if the damage was already noted
- Reflects on the route and any contact or sounds, files an ICBC claim and gives the claim number and details to the manager, and participates in any follow up or retraining

questions.text: Describe a General, Critical, and Reportable Incident and how you would handle them?
questions.answerKey:
- General incident: internal report for events not deemed critical, such as property damage by a person supported or minor illness not needing emergency care; notify manager and complete the GIR, which helps track patterns before they escalate
- Critical incident: involves emergency services such as police, ambulance, fire or hospital; ensure safety, notify manager immediately, complete the CIR before leaving shift
- Reportable incident: an incident occurring in a licensed home; ensure safety, report to the manager immediately, complete the report before leaving work
- In all cases the first step is the immediate safety and wellbeing of the person supported and others present
- Reports written same shift, factual and objective, describing what was observed rather than opinion or blame
- Recognises duty to report suspected abuse or neglect externally, separate from internal incident reporting

questions.text: Describe situations where you should contact your manager, during or after working hours? What are some situations where you should not contact your manager after hours?
questions.answerKey:
- Contact during or after hours for: you are ill or have an emergency and must leave shift, relieving staff has not arrived, a person supported needs hospital or emergency services, a medication error, a significant or unusual behaviour or incident, an issue with a community member, a vehicle accident
- Understands anything affecting the immediate safety, health or coverage of a person supported cannot wait
- Does not call after hours for routine administrative matters: relieving staff running a minute late, vacation requests, paystub questions, a memo in the communication book, asking whether they can do some baking
- Holds non urgent items for the next business day, the communication book or a team meeting
- Shows judgement about urgency rather than either escalating everything or hesitating to call when it matters

questions.text: What is the protocol for administering PRN medication?
questions.answerKey:
- Checks the MAR binder and the PRN approval form before giving anything
- Matches the written PRN order or protocol to the reason the medication is being considered, and tries any non medication strategies the protocol calls for first
- Follows standard medication administration practice, including the required checks and recording the dose
- Monitors the person afterward for effect and any adverse reaction
- Documents in the nurse's notes on oneMAR or the reverse of the paper MAR, including the reason given and the outcome
- Informs the manager where required, and reports a medication error immediately if one occurs

questions.text: How would you handle a conflict with a coworker? What steps would you take to resolve it?
questions.answerKey:
- Goes directly to the coworker first, in private and at a calm moment, and keeps it to the specific issue rather than the person
- Checks own regulation and assumptions before the conversation, and listens to the coworker's view rather than arriving to win
- Offers concrete solutions, for example how shift handover, task splitting or communication with the person supported will work going forward
- Brings it to the manager if it is not resolved, and participates openly in conflict resolution or mediation
- Does not gossip about it with other staff, family or people supported, and does not recruit others to take a side
- Keeps the focus on consistency of support for the person supported, so team conflict does not spill into the home

questions.text: Who is your current manager that we can contact for an internal reference?
questions.answerKey:
- Names their current manager and program or home
- Confirms current contact details for that manager
- Confirms whether the manager is aware of the application and consent to contact them
- Note any previous Milieu manager to contact if the current one is new to the role or the candidate has recently transferred

questions.text: You were driving the company vehicle, and when you return to the home, you notice physical damage. What steps do you take and what reporting is required?
questions.answerKey:
- Checks first whether anyone was in the vehicle or involved, and that the person supported and staff are safe and not injured
- Reports it to the manager or on call right away rather than waiting for the next shift or hoping it is noticed later
- Is honest and does not minimise, even if unsure whether they caused the damage or when it happened
- Documents the damage in writing with date, time, location, what was noticed and any relevant detail, including photos if that is how the program records it, and completes the required incident report
- Records it in the vehicle log or maintenance record and follows manager direction on repair, insurance or ICBC reporting, and does not use the vehicle if it is unsafe to drive
- Takes part in follow up review of how it happened and what would prevent it, without blaming other staff

name: Youth Internal
description: Internal posting for youth services staff. The paper form scores 14 questions at 5 points each, 70% to pass.

questions.text: Do you have any conditions or previous injuries that might impact your ability to perform this role?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms whether there is anything that would limit physical demands of the role such as Mandt physical intervention, standing shifts, driving, or lifting
- States clearly whether any accommodation is being requested and what it would be
- Confirms ability to do overnight or awake shifts if relevant to the posting
- Interviewer follow up: note any accommodation request for manager and confirm it is handled through the proper process, no medical detail beyond what the candidate offers

questions.text: Some of our homes are single staffed, are you comfortable supporting youth one to one?
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes or no on working alone with youth, including evenings, overnights and weekends
- Describes how they stay safe alone: knowing the safety plan, exit routes, phone charged, checking in with on call
- Names when they would call the on call manager, another staff, or emergency services rather than manage alone
- Comfortable making decisions in the moment and documenting them for the next shift
- Realistic about the isolation of single staffing and how they keep themselves regulated across a shift

questions.text: Have you ever been involved in a protocol with Milieu or another agency? Yes: No: (if yes, have them provide information about this)
questions.answerKey:
- Direct yes or no answer without deflection
- If yes: agency involved, approximate date, nature of the allegation, and outcome or whether it is still open
- Describes their own role and how they participated in the process, for example cooperating with the investigation and following any direction given
- Reflects on what changed in their practice afterwards without minimising or blaming the youth
- Interviewer follow up: record details and pass to manager for verification

questions.text: The position may require you to provide outreach supports to youth. What do you think this would involve? Do you have experience with this and would you be comfortable doing so?
questions.answerKey:
- Meeting youth where they are at in the community rather than expecting them to come to an office or home
- Locating youth and confirming their safety, checking basic needs such as food, clothing, shelter and health
- Connecting youth to community resources and supporting them to access services
- Uses the contact to build rapport over time, person centred and led by what the youth identifies as important
- Describes safety practice in community: knows the plan for the shift, communicates location, keeps professional boundaries in public and in vehicles
- Gives concrete prior experience and states plainly whether they are comfortable doing this work

questions.text: How do you assess and maintain your own safety while still being supportive to a youth in crisis?
questions.answerKey:
- Keeps RADAR running throughout the shift: recognise, assess, decide, act, review
- Scans the environment at the start of shift and again as soon as escalation begins, noting exits, objects and other people present
- Reads and follows the individual support guidelines, behaviour support plan and safety plan before working with the youth
- Maintains position and distance that keeps them safe while staying available and calm
- Maintains professional boundaries and monitors their own regulation, stepping back or handing over when needed
- Knows when to call for assistance: on call manager, second staff, police or ambulance, and documents afterwards

questions.text: What is your experience and knowledge working with young people who use substances
questions.answerKey:
- Supportive and non judgemental stance, harm reduction rather than punishment or moralising
- Supports the youth to explore resources and options at their own pace
- Knows and follows the house or centre protocols around substances on site
- Stays non confrontational when a youth is under the influence, avoids interrogation and power struggles, holds conversations for when they are regulated
- Assesses current health status and decides whether medical support is needed
- Recognises signs of overdose, uses Narcan and calls 911, and completes the incident reporting that follows

questions.text: How would you provide support if a youth has a history of trauma and attachment difficulties
questions.answerKey:
- Trauma informed approach: avoids retraumatising, does not require the youth to repeat their story to multiple people, stays aware of possible triggers
- Builds rapport at the youth's pace through consistency, predictability and follow through rather than forcing attachment or closeness
- Self aware and regulated, prepared for testing behaviour, rejection or push and pull, and does not take it personally
- Authentic and honest in responses, does not over promise what they can offer
- Maintains professional boundaries, including around personal disclosure, contact outside shifts and favouritism
- Works from the ISP and support guidelines, brings observations to the team and manager rather than working in isolation

questions.text: The youth we support sometimes have emotional outbursts that escalate into yelling and aggression. What strategies have you used to de-escalate a situation like this?
questions.answerKey:
- Knows the youth's support strategies, triggers and communication style ahead of time from the plan and the team
- Remains neutral, calm and low in tone and volume, reduces demands and questions during the escalation
- Follows the behaviour support and safety plan rather than improvising
- Maintains appropriate distance and gives space, keeps exits clear
- Concrete strategies: redirect to a quiet space, deep breathing, calming music, offering a walk or a drink, moving other youth out of the area
- Documents afterwards and debriefs with the team so strategies can be adjusted

questions.text: If a youth becomes verbally aggressive toward you during an outing. How would you respond?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives space and time, keeps a safe distance while keeping eyes on the youth
- Disengages from the content of the comments, does not argue, correct or respond to insults
- Avoids power struggles and public confrontation, does not use ultimatums or threats about consequences
- Scans the environment for risks and bystanders, considers moving to a quieter area or returning to the vehicle or home
- Follows the youth's support plan and has a proactive plan for what they will do if it escalates further, including who they would call
- Revisits it later when the youth is at baseline, and documents the incident

questions.text: What steps would you take immediately after a crisis to re-establish a supportive connection with them?
questions.answerKey:
- Assesses whether the youth has actually returned to baseline before approaching, allows time
- Re engages with something low demand and normal, for example a snack, a task together or a drive, no lecturing
- Debriefs only if it is part of the plan and the youth can hold it without re-escalating, otherwise leaves it for later
- Repairs the relationship: makes clear the youth is not in trouble with them and the relationship is intact
- Redirects back to the daily schedule and routine
- Checks their own regulation, debriefs with the team or manager, and completes incident documentation

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to set a firm boundary with a youth and how they responded
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a real example with a specific youth, the boundary set and how the youth actually responded, including if it went poorly
- Holds house rules or centre expectations with a trauma informed lens rather than rigid rule enforcement
- Stays calm and neutral while the youth pushes back, does not escalate to match them
- Transparent about the reason for the boundary and states it simply and once
- Adapts and offers choice or alternatives where possible while still holding the boundary, avoids power struggles
- Follows through consistently and repairs the relationship afterwards

questions.text: You notice a youth hasn't showered or engaged in hygiene in several days and refuses when you suggest it. How would you support them?
questions.answerKey:
- Considers what might be behind the refusal: sensory issues, trauma history, depression, privacy or body image, and checks the support plan and team knowledge
- Approaches it without shaming, in private, and does not turn it into a power struggle or a condition for other activities
- Makes it more appealing and person centred: shopping together for products they like, preferred water temperature, music, time of day that works for them
- Ensures the bathroom is clean, private and welcoming, and offers to do the routine alongside them or model it first
- Breaks it into small steps and builds it into a consistent daily routine rather than expecting a full shower straight away
- Documents patterns and raises ongoing refusal or health concerns with the manager or team

questions.text: How would you handle a conflict with a coworker? What steps would you take to resolve it?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts with self reflection on their own part in the situation before approaching anyone
- Goes directly to the coworker first, in private and at a calm time, keeping it to the issue and its impact on the shift or the youth rather than the person
- Brings suggested solutions, not just a complaint, and checks what the coworker sees differently
- Escalates to the manager if it is not resolved, or sooner if it affects the safety or consistency of support for a youth
- Participates openly in a facilitated conflict resolution process and follows through on what was agreed
- Keeps it off the floor: no venting to other staff or in front of youth, no drawing coworkers onto one side

questions.text: Describe situations where you should contact your manager, during or after working hours? What are some situations where you should not contact your manager after hours?
questions.answerKey:
- Contact during or after hours when there is a health or safety issue: a youth needing hospital or ambulance, a medication error, injury, police involvement, a significant or unusual behaviour, elopement or absence from the program, an incident with a community member, a vehicle accident
- Contact for coverage problems that leave a shift unstaffed: relief staff has not arrived, or the candidate becomes ill or has an emergency and cannot finish the shift
- Recognises single staffed sites mean the manager is the backup and hesitating to call is a bigger risk than calling unnecessarily
- Does not call after hours for administrative or non urgent matters: vacation requests, payroll or paystub questions, a memo in the communication book, routine questions such as baking or an activity idea, relief staff running a minute or two late
- Holds non urgent items for the next shift, the communication book, or a scheduled check in with the manager
- Can articulate the test they use: is this a risk to a youth, to staff, or to the shift being covered

questions.text: Describe some of the types of documentation we are required to keep and why it is important?
questions.answerKey:
- Names concrete documents from the setting: daily logs or contact notes, ISPs and goal progress, incident reports, intake forms, progress reports; in homes also personal charting such as body checks, bowel movements, seizures and weight, overnight checks, vehicle checks and mileage
- Explains why: continuity so the next shift knows what happened, consistency of support, tracking progress toward a youth's goals, medical and health tracking, health and safety, and meeting MCFD and licensing standards
- Understands documentation is a legal record: factual, objective, timely, written in the youth's own terms rather than opinion or labels
- Knows external reporting to MCFD is required, including after hours, for incidents and serious incidents, and that reporting is immediate rather than left to the end of shift
- Gives examples of reportable events: injury, police or ambulance attendance, behaviour involving property damage, breach of conditions, absence from the program or missing youth
- Distinguishes general, critical and reportable incidents and knows duty to report sits with them personally, not only with the manager

questions.text: Give an example of some situations that a protocol would be called for
questions.answerKey:
- Any allegation of abuse or neglect involving a youth
- Staff found sleeping on shift, or leaving a youth unattended in the home or community
- Late reporting, or failure to report, for example not passing on a disclosure a youth made
- Inappropriate comments, reactions or boundary issues with a youth
- Understands a protocol is an MCFD or internal investigation of an allegation, that they cooperate fully and do not investigate or discuss it with others, and that a protocol being called is not a finding of guilt
- Knows to report the concern to the manager immediately even when it involves a coworker or themselves

name: Vocational Counsellor
description: Internal posting for Vocational Counsellor and Employment Specialist. 19 scored questions plus supplemental questions that carry no score.

questions.text: Do you have a valid Class 5 BCDL? YES or
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm yes or no to a valid Class 5 BC driver's licence, and note whether they have a reliable vehicle and business class insurance for community driving
- If they hold a Class 7N and are applying for a day position, explain they would start in a temporary position and have three months to obtain the Class 5
- If they hold neither, explain courteously that they do not qualify for a day position and encourage them to apply to other vacant postings
- Follow up on abstract or licence check requirements as part of the standard hiring screen

questions.text: Tell me what you know about the role of a Vocational Counsellor & Employment Consultant
questions.answerKey:
- Assesses skills, strengths, interests, abilities, personality and values to help a person supported identify careers that fit them
- Builds job readiness: resumes, cover letters, portfolios, interview practice, job search strategies and networking
- Explores career options, labour market trends, training, certifications, apprenticeships and education pathways, and supports people through transitions
- Connects people to community resources, funding programs and support services, and advocates for workplace accommodations
- Develops relationships with local employers and businesses, understands their staffing needs and matches job seekers to them
- Motivates and encourages, keeping the person's own choices and goals at the centre rather than pushing a placement

questions.text: What's the difference between a Vocational Counsellor and a Community Support Worker?
questions.answerKey:
- Vocational Counsellor focuses on employment and career development: assessment, career planning, job readiness, labour market guidance and sustainable employment or education outcomes
- Vocational Counsellor works with barriers to entering or returning to work, and liaises directly with employers
- Community Support Worker focuses on day to day living: life skills, routines, community participation, personal support and overall wellbeing
- Community Support Worker supports stability and independence in the person's home and community, including connecting to resources and responding to crisis
- Recognises the roles overlap and work together around the same person supported and their ISP, with shared documentation and communication

questions.text: Please Explain the difference between traditional Job Seeking and Supported Employment
questions.answerKey:
- Traditional job seeking is self directed: the person finds postings, applies, interviews and negotiates on their own with minimal outside support
- Employers in that process expect applicants to already have the skills, experience and readiness for the role
- Supported employment is individualised and guided, designed for people facing barriers to employment
- Supported employment includes job matching to the person's strengths and interests, job coaching on site, arranging accommodations, and employer education
- Support continues after hire with long term follow up and retention checks, faded as the person gains independence
- Both aim at real, competitive, paid work in the community, not segregated or make work activity

questions.text: What does it mean to be a "job coach" or "life coach"?
questions.answerKey:
- Job coach gives individualised, hands on support at the work site: teaching tasks, modelling, prompting, and building workplace skills and confidence
- Helps the person understand employer expectations, workplace culture and routines, and problem solves challenges as they arise
- Works with the employer on job match, explaining accommodations and supporting a smooth onboarding
- Plans deliberately to fade support as the person becomes more independent, aiming for long term sustainable employment
- Life coaching side: helping the person identify strengths, clarify values, set achievable goals and work through obstacles, with encouragement and accountability
- Empowers the person to own their choices rather than making decisions for them, and holds professional boundaries while doing it

questions.text: What would you say to a parent who says their son/daughter is not ready for employment?
questions.answerKey:
- Listens first and validates the parent's concern without dismissing it, recognising they often carry real history of past setbacks or worry about safety and benefits
- Explains that readiness is developmental and built through experience rather than something a person either has or does not have
- Keeps the person supported at the centre and asks what they want, honouring self determination while keeping the family engaged
- Offers low risk starting points such as volunteering, job shadowing, work experience or a few hours part time
- Reassures the parent about the ongoing coaching, monitoring and employer contact that comes with supported employment
- Agrees to keep the parent informed and to revisit the conversation, rather than pressing for a decision in the moment

questions.text: Explain that employment support is tailored to each person, focusing on building skills, confidence, and independence at their own pace
What do you think the appropriate clothing is for you to wear as a Job Developer going to an office setting, versus you working as a job coach at a warehouse?
questions.answerKey:
- Office or job development: business casual, such as a clean shirt, blouse or polo, pants, blazer or cardigan, closed toe shoes
- Warehouse or job coaching on site: work pants or jeans, t shirt or long sleeves, plus required safety gear such as steel toe boots, hi vis vest, gloves, eye and ear protection or hard hat
- Follows the employer's site requirements, since PPE expectations vary by workplace
- In all settings neat, clean and professional, avoiding logos, shorts or revealing clothing
- Recognises they represent both Milieu and the person supported to the employer, and dresses to be approachable and credible

questions.text: How would you know when someone has found the job that is right for them?
questions.answerKey:
- The person expresses satisfaction and comfort in the role and shows enjoyment or pride in the work
- The job uses their actual strengths, interests and abilities so they can contribute meaningfully
- Needed accommodations and supports are in place and working at the site
- They are consistently engaged, punctual, reliable and able to manage the tasks without undue stress or burnout
- The environment, routines and social expectations fit their preferences, and they are included by co-workers
- Employer check ins are positive, and over time there are signs of learning, growing confidence and reduced need for coaching

questions.text: How would you develop a relationship with a potential employer?
questions.answerKey:
- Researches the business first: mission, values, culture, hours and staffing needs, so the approach is informed
- Makes professional contact by email, phone, drop in or networking events, introducing themselves and the service clearly
- Asks questions and listens to the employer's hiring challenges and workplace expectations rather than leading with a pitch
- Frames it as a business solution: how the job seeker and the ongoing coaching support meet the employer's needs, including any wage or funding supports available
- Maintains consistent, non intrusive follow up with updates and check ins after placement
- Builds credibility over time through reliability, responsiveness and honest communication when problems arise, and respects the privacy of the person supported by sharing only what is needed

questions.text: Describe some strategies you'd use to secure job placements
questions.answerKey:
- Starts with the job seeker: identifies skills, strengths, interests and barriers, and builds resume, cover letter and online profiles such as Indeed or LinkedIn
- Prepares the person through interview practice, job fairs and realistic conversations about hours, transport and supports needed
- Does active employer research and networking, targeting businesses that fit the person's skills and interests, including chamber events, job fairs and warm referrals
- Job matches deliberately rather than mass applying, and may propose a customised or carved role to fit the employer's unfilled tasks
- Advocates directly to employers, explaining the person's contribution and how accommodations and job coaching will work
- Follows up with both the employer and the person supported after placement to support retention, and uses community and online resources to keep a pipeline of leads

questions.text: If the person you are job coaching is unable to attend work what do you think your responsibility is as a job coach?
questions.answerKey:
- Ensures the employer is notified promptly following the workplace's call in procedure, and makes the call on the person's behalf if they are unable to do it themselves
- Coaches the person toward doing that call independently over time, so absence reporting becomes a skill they own
- Looks into what is behind the absence, such as health, transportation, sensory overload, anxiety or a scheduling conflict, without assuming or blaming
- Works with the person on supports or accommodations that prevent a repeat, adjusting the plan or hours if needed
- Checks in afterward with encouragement and helps them prepare to return to work confidently
- Keeps the employer relationship positive and expectations clear, documents the absence and the follow up, and lets the manager and the person's support team know if a pattern is emerging

questions.text: A job seeker is having challenges with performing their job at a reasonable speed. How might you support them with this?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts by observing the actual task on site and talking with the person supported to find out what is getting in the way: skill gap, unclear instructions, fatigue, distraction, anxiety, or a task that was never a good fit
- Breaks the job into smaller steps, sequences and prioritises them, and uses concrete tools such as checklists, visual sequences, timers or a set routine rather than telling the person to hurry
- Provides hands on coaching and repeated practice on the specific steps that slow the person down, fading support as speed and confidence build
- Works with the employer on practical accommodations such as adjusted workload, quieter area, staggered deadlines, or reordered duties, framed around what the employer needs to run the business
- Names progress specifically and keeps the person supported in the driver's seat about goals and pace, checking whether they want the job as it stands
- If pace remains a barrier after support, has an honest three way conversation about reassigning tasks or finding a better matched role, without framing it as failure

questions.text: An employer calls you to say a supported employee is taking their break for 45 minutes instead of 15 minutes. However, when you were coaching last week, you observed the employee take their break at the right time and for 15 minutes. What do you do?
questions.answerKey:
- Thanks the employer, listens without becoming defensive, and asks for specifics: which days, what time, how often, who observed it, has it been raised with the person supported
- Treats one observation as a snapshot rather than proof either way, and arranges to observe again at the times the employer describes
- Talks with the person supported directly, supportively and without accusation, asking what breaks look like for them and checking whether they can tell time, read the schedule, or are being kept talking by coworkers
- Considers practical explanations: shift or break time changed, clock or timer not visible, new supervisor, transit or medication routine, a change in the person's health
- Puts a simple support in place if needed, such as a timer, phone alarm, visual reminder or a coworker cue, and agrees with the employer how it will be reviewed
- Documents the employer contact, observations and plan, follows up with both parties, and lets the manager know if the concern continues or escalates

questions.text: How might you deal with an employer/person in community who doesn't believe that a person with a disability can have paid employment?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays curious and non defensive, asks what the concern actually is, and separates a myth from a genuine business worry such as cost, safety, supervision time or productivity
- Speaks to the specific person: their skills, work history, reliability and what tasks they can do well, rather than arguing about disability in the abstract
- Uses concrete examples of other supported placements and outcomes, and speaks to the employer in business language about turnover, coverage and quality
- Offers a low risk way to test it, such as a job trial, job shadow, work experience or a discrete set of tasks, backed by job coaching at no cost to the employer
- Keeps the door open rather than pushing for a decision, follows up, and builds the relationship over time; does not disclose personal or medical information the person supported has not consented to share
- Keeps the person supported informed and involved in how they are represented, respecting their choice about disclosure

questions.text: Explain Workplace Supports and Accommodations: Discuss how supports, training, or accommodations can help the employee succeed while minimizing disruption for the employer
What do you think "independence" means in the context of employment supports?
questions.answerKey:
- Independence is about the person supported having control and choice in their working life, not about the absence of support
- Includes decision making: what job to pursue, what hours, whether to disclose, when to ask for a change
- Includes self advocacy: being able to ask a supervisor a question, request an accommodation, or say when something is not working
- Builds skills and natural supports at the workplace so coworkers and supervisors, rather than the coach, become the day to day support
- Involves deliberately fading coaching and reviewing support levels so the arrangement does not create dependency on the counsellor
- Recognises that ongoing supports can still be part of an independent working life; independence looks different for each person supported

questions.text: Describe what you would do if the person you are supporting didn't show up at your designated meeting place?
questions.answerKey:
- Waits a reasonable time and first checks the basics: confirmed time and location, recent messages, whether the meeting place changed
- Attempts contact by phone or text in a non blaming way, focused on whether the person supported is safe
- If there is no response, follows the direction in that person's support guidelines, contacts the emergency or alternate contacts, and notifies the manager for direction rather than searching indefinitely alone
- Considers safety indicators known for that person, such as health conditions or previous concerns, and escalates promptly if there is reason to worry
- Once contact is made, explores the barrier without judgement (transit, money, sleep, health, anxiety about the job) and problem solves reminders or a different meeting point
- Documents the missed meeting, contact attempts and outcome, informs the manager, and reschedules

questions.text: You are meeting the person at their home to take public transit together, to their place of work as part of transit coaching. You arrive and you find the front door open, you knock and you hear a "come in" so you walk in. You see the person you are supporting using drugs. What do you do?
questions.answerKey:
- Checks safety first for themselves, the person supported and anyone else present, and calls emergency services if the person is unresponsive or showing signs of overdose; knows naloxone use if trained and available
- Stays calm and neutral, does not lecture, confront or shame; recognises the person supported is an adult with the right to make their own choices
- Recognises the transit coaching cannot safely go ahead, says so matter of factly, and supports the person to call in to work or reschedule
- Leaves the home if the environment is unsafe or others present pose a risk, and does not stay to manage it alone
- Contacts the manager the same day for direction and documents factual observations only, without assumptions or diagnostic language
- Follows up later in line with the person's own goals and support plan, keeping the working relationship and professional boundaries intact

questions.text: You are meeting with the person you support today to work on their Employment plan, however they shared they got evicted from their place this morning. What do you do?
questions.answerKey:
- Sets the employment plan aside and responds to the immediate need: does the person supported have somewhere safe to sleep tonight, their medication, belongings and money
- Contacts the manager promptly to advise of the change in priority and to get direction on scope and next steps
- Knows or finds the relevant supports: shelter and housing intake, crisis lines, after hours services, income assistance, and the person's own natural supports
- Involves the person supported in every decision, offers options rather than directing, and checks how they are coping emotionally
- Documents what happened, what was offered and what was arranged, and hands over clearly to the manager, on call or next worker so nothing is dropped
- Keeps professional boundaries: does not house the person, lend money or take on tasks outside the role, and returns to employment planning once housing is stabilised, recognising employment may be affected

questions.text: What does professionalism mean to you?
questions.answerKey:
- Reliability: shows up on time, does what they said they would, and tells the manager early when they cannot
- Ethical conduct: confidentiality, honesty about mistakes, no conflicts of interest, working within their role and scope
- Respect toward people supported, families, employers, coworkers and funders, including how they speak about people when they are not present
- Clear boundaries: warm and relational without becoming a friend, no personal favours, money or social media contact
- Clear communication and documentation, including raising concerns through the right channel rather than venting
- Self regulation: manages their own reaction under pressure, handles disagreement calmly, seeks supervision and feedback
- Presents appropriately for the setting, including workplaces where they represent the person supported and the agency

questions.text: Describe your administration skills and experience. Please share specific examples of tasks you've handled and programs you are comfortable using (ie Word, Outlook, Excel, PowerPoint, managing schedules, creating documents, creating presentations etc.)
questions.answerKey:
- Gives concrete examples of past administrative work rather than general statements: case notes, reports, referrals, scheduling, minutes, correspondence
- Names specific software and their actual comfort level with each, for example Word, Outlook, Excel, PowerPoint, and any database or case management system used
- Describes how they organise and prioritise competing tasks and meet reporting timelines while carrying a caseload
- Shows accuracy and attention to detail in documentation and data entry, and understands notes may be read by funders or in a review
- Demonstrates awareness of privacy and confidentiality when handling personal information about people supported
- Gives an example of improving or streamlining a process, or of catching and correcting an administrative error

questions.text: What personal characteristics do you have that you believe are important to being an Employment Counsellor?
questions.answerKey:
- Empathy and genuine listening, able to hear what the person supported wants from work rather than deciding for them
- Patience and persistence through slow progress, setbacks, job losses and repeated employer contact
- Clear plain language communication, and comfort switching between talking with a person supported, a family, and an employer
- Creativity and problem solving in job matching, task carving and working around barriers
- Organisation across a caseload: tracking progress, follow ups and multiple employer relationships
- Optimism and belief in employability, balanced with honesty; plus integrity, confidentiality and self awareness about their own boundaries and biases

questions.text: What is your comfort level with deadlines and how do you manage them?
questions.answerKey:
- States a realistic comfort level and backs it with an example of a deadline they managed or missed and what they did about it
- Describes a concrete system: calendar, task list, reminders, blocking time for documentation rather than leaving it to the end
- Prioritises when demands compete, and recognises that a safety or crisis issue with a person supported takes precedence over paperwork
- Communicates early with the manager when a deadline is at risk instead of going quiet or handing in rushed work
- Understands deadlines connect to funders, employers and people supported, so late reports have real consequences for others
- Stays steady under time pressure and does not let deadline stress spill into contact with people supported

questions.text: Describe your communication style
questions.answerKey:
- Conveys information clearly and respectfully to different audiences: people supported, families, employers, co-workers and supervisors
- Listens actively, checks understanding rather than assuming, and responds to what the person is actually asking for
- Adapts style to the person and situation, including plain language, extra time, visual or written supports for people with diversabilities
- Shows empathy and patience, and stays calm and non-defensive in difficult or emotional conversations
- Handles conflict directly and diplomatically, and knows when a conversation needs a manager involved
- Names their own preferred way of communicating and receiving information, including feedback

questions.text: Due to the nature of this role (being flexible to support people/employers in afternoon/evenings), do you have a secondary job that we should be aware of? (Please get details of their position- days/hours, etc.)
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm whether there is other employment, and record employer, position, days and hours
- Confirm any conflict with afternoon and evening availability, which this role requires for supporting people and employers
- Note any commitment to on-call, rotating or unpredictable shifts elsewhere
- Flag any actual or perceived conflict of interest with Milieu, funders or partner employers for follow-up

questions.text: Do you have any upcoming vacations/requested dates off that we should be aware of?
questions.answerKey:
- Record specific dates already booked or requested, including travel
- Note whether any dates fall within orientation or training
- Confirm how much notice they can give for future time off requests

questions.text: Based on this interview, are you still interested in the position?
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes or no, with any reservations named
- Any conditions attached, such as hours, wage, location or travel across service areas
- Note remaining questions the candidate has about the role that need follow-up

questions.text: When can you start?
questions.answerKey:
- Specific available start date
- Notice period owed to a current employer
- Availability for orientation and required training dates
- Status of criminal record check, driver's abstract, licence and other clearances that affect start date

questions.text: Do you have any conditions or previous injuries that might impact your ability to perform this role?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can perform the role's physical and practical demands, including driving, community travel and job site support
- Note any accommodation the candidate identifies as needed, without asking for diagnostic or medical detail
- Flag anything requiring follow-up through the appropriate HR or accommodation process

name: Adult Internal to Youth
description: For Milieu adult services staff applying to work with youth.

questions.text: Tell us about your approach to caregiving i.e. Communication style, conflict resolution skills, appropriate discipline techniques?
questions.answerKey:
- Relationship first: builds rapport and predictability before expecting cooperation, uses calm tone, plain language and choices rather than commands
- Names that discipline in this context means natural and logical consequences, coaching and repair, never physical discipline, withholding food, contact or belongings, or shaming
- Conflict resolution that avoids power struggles: gives space and time, keeps the issue small, revisits once everyone is regulated
- Works from the youth's plan and individual support guidelines and stays consistent with the rest of the team rather than making private deals
- Shows awareness of own triggers and regulation, and willingness to hand off to a co-worker or call the manager when needed
- Concrete example from their own caregiving or support experience

questions.text: The youth we support come into our services for various reasons, what are some of the challenges and barriers that may have contributed to the youth needing services? What would be helpful?
questions.answerKey:
- Names realistic contributors: abuse or neglect, family breakdown, multiple placements, grief and loss, poverty and housing instability, substance use in the home, parental mental health, FASD or other diversabilities, unmet school needs
- Recognises systemic barriers including racism, the ongoing impact of residential schools and child welfare on Indigenous families, immigration and language barriers, and 2SLGBTQ+ youth being unsupported at home
- Understands attachment and trauma responses: mistrust of adults, testing behaviour, difficulty regulating, and that this is protective rather than personal
- Helpful supports named concretely: stability and routine, one consistent trusting relationship, cultural and family connection, school and counselling supports, life skills and transition to adulthood planning
- Frames youth by strengths and interests rather than by deficits or diagnosis

questions.text: Tell us what you think you'd be doing in a typical shift?
questions.answerKey:
- Shift handover and reading the log and communication book at the start, documenting and passing on at the end
- Daily rhythm: wake ups, meals and cooking, school or program transport, appointments, chores and life skills, curfew and bedtime routines
- Medication administration and documentation including PRN, plus health and safety checks of the home
- Relationship and recreation time: being present, one to one conversation, community activities, homework support
- Documentation throughout: shift notes, general, critical or reportable incidents, following the ISP and safety or behaviour support plans
- Realistic view of single staffed homes: managing alone, phoning the on call manager or supervisor when something escalates

questions.text: Please describe the rights of children and youth in care?
questions.answerKey:
- To be safe, and free from abuse, neglect, physical discipline and discrimination
- To be told about their rights, to have a say in decisions and plans about them, and to have their views taken seriously
- Privacy and confidentiality of their information, and privacy of their belongings and space within safety limits
- Contact with family, friends, community, culture, spirituality and language, and support to maintain Indigenous identity and connection
- Access to food, clothing, education, health and dental care, and to a lawyer, advocate or the Representative for Children and Youth
- To complain without fear of consequence, and to be supported to make that complaint

questions.text: If you witnessed something that breeched our policies or rights of children in care what would you do? (looking to see if they know procedure for Duty to Report)
questions.answerKey:
- Ensures the youth is safe first and interrupts the situation if it is still happening
- States clearly that duty to report is a legal obligation held by them personally and cannot be delegated or passed off to a co-worker
- Reports to the manager or supervisor, and reports directly to MCFD or the child protection line where a child's safety is involved, regardless of what the manager says
- Documents factually and promptly: what was seen and heard, times, who was present, no opinion or speculation, and completes the incident report at the correct tier
- Understands a protocol investigation may follow, stays cooperative, keeps the matter confidential and does not investigate or confront on their own
- Does not let loyalty to a co-worker, being new, or being internal to the agency stop the report

questions.text: Tell us about your experience working with people who sometimes communicate using challenging behaviour. What did it look like? What do you think the person was trying to communicate?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a real situation concretely: what happened before, what the behaviour looked like, how long, how it ended
- Treats the behaviour as communication and identifies the likely need: pain or illness, sensory overload, fear, hunger or fatigue, grief, wanting control or connection, being asked something they could not do or understand
- Notes antecedents and patterns rather than describing the person as difficult, and uses non judgemental language
- Describes their own response: kept calm, lowered voice and demands, gave space and time, kept themselves and others safe, avoided a power struggle
- References working from the person's support guidelines and behaviour support or safety plan, and Mandt as a last resort after de-escalation
- Reflects on their own regulation during and after the incident, and debriefing afterward

questions.text: What could have been done to support this person to get their needs met without having them use challenging behaviour? (HR - Give Details)
questions.answerKey:
- Identifies proactive changes: predictable routine, advance warning of transitions, offering real choices, reducing demands and noise, meeting physical needs earlier
- Teaching and honouring another way to communicate the same need, and responding to it consistently so the youth learns it works
- Getting to know the person's history, triggers and early warning signs, and intervening at the early stage rather than at crisis
- Team consistency: everyone using the same approach, updating the ISP or behaviour support plan, raising it with the manager and other professionals
- Honest reflection on what they or the team would do differently, including their own tone, timing or assumptions

questions.text: If a youth were to come to you and disclose their history or experience of abuse and or trauma. How would you respond to this disclosure?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays calm and present, listens without reacting visibly, believes the youth and thanks them for telling
- Lets the youth lead and tell it at their own pace, does not interview, probe for detail, or ask leading or why questions
- Does not promise confidentiality, explains gently and honestly that they have to pass this on to keep them safe and what will happen next
- Uses the youth's own words when documenting, factually and as soon as possible, and reports to the manager and to MCFD as duty to report requires
- Keeps the youth supported after the disclosure: stays with them, offers comfort and normal routine, does not treat them differently
- Recognises the impact on themselves and seeks debrief or supervision

questions.text: If the youth you are working with comes to you and tell you they have been sexually assaulted or abused by someone? What would you do and how would you respond to this situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Addresses immediate safety and medical need first, including whether the person who caused harm has access to the youth right now
- Listens, believes, does not question or investigate, does not ask for details, preserves the youth's own words
- Explains that they must report, does not promise to keep it secret, and follows through on duty to report to MCFD and police as required, plus the manager or on call
- Preserves evidence where relevant, for example does not encourage washing or changing clothes, and supports the youth to access medical care or a sexual assault service
- Documents factually and promptly and completes the reportable incident process
- Stays with the youth, follows their lead on what feels safe, and arranges follow up support and their own debrief

questions.text: In your role as a staff, you may experience the youth using racial slurs towards you. How would you cope with this scenario?
questions.answerKey:
- Does not retaliate, argue or match the escalation, keeps their own regulation and body language calm
- Names in the moment that the language is not okay while staying in relationship, without shaming or lecturing during the crisis
- Gives space, keeps everyone safe, and returns to the conversation once the youth is regulated to repair and talk about impact
- Recognises the behaviour often reflects distress, testing or learned language rather than a fixed belief, without excusing racism
- Knows they are allowed to be affected: tells the manager, debriefs with the team, asks for support, and does not carry it alone
- Documents the incident and raises it with the team so the response is consistent and the youth gets follow up

questions.text: If a youth is talking to you about killing themselves, how would you handle this situation? And would you do anything different if they actually attempted to kill themselves?
questions.answerKey:
- Takes all talk of suicide seriously, stays with the youth, listens without judgement or panic, and does not minimise or promise secrecy
- Asks directly and calmly about intent, plan and means, and removes or reduces access to means where safe to do so
- Notifies the manager or on call right away and follows the youth's safety plan, involving MCFD, crisis line, or 911 as the risk level requires
- Maintains supervision and does not leave the youth alone until the risk is assessed and a plan is in place
- If an attempt occurs: calls 911 and gives first aid within their training, stays with the youth, then reports as a critical or reportable incident and completes documentation
- Recognises the emotional impact on themselves, debriefs, and plans follow up support and increased monitoring for the youth

questions.text: How would you respond to witnessing a youth self-harming or displaying self-injurious behavior (e.g., cutting or hitting their head against the wall)?
questions.answerKey:
- Responds calmly without shock, disgust or ultimatums, and avoids a power struggle over stopping the behaviour
- Attends to physical safety and first aid, seeks medical attention where injury requires it, and reduces access to means where possible
- Understands self harm as a coping strategy for unbearable feeling, and stays curious about the need behind it rather than treating it as manipulation
- Follows the youth's safety or behaviour support plan, offers connection, distraction and alternatives once the youth is calmer, and checks for suicidal intent
- Notifies the manager or on call, documents factually and completes the incident report at the correct tier
- Debriefs with the youth and the team afterward, plans ongoing supports, and attends to their own reaction

questions.text: If you had to take a youth to the hospital for any reason would you be okay with supporting the youth in the hospital?
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes to staying with the youth for the length of the wait, including long ER waits and shift extensions arranged with the manager
- Notifies the manager or on call right away and follows the incident reporting process for the tier of incident
- Brings and shares relevant information: medications, allergies, individual support guidelines, safety or behaviour support plan, consent and guardianship details, MCFD social worker contact
- Supports the youth through the wait: stays calm, explains what is happening, advocates so the youth is heard by staff, respects their privacy and dignity
- Documents the visit, discharge instructions and any follow up appointments, and hands over clearly to the next shift

questions.text: There are times you will have to deal with police interactions regarding the youth you are supporting. If this was the case, how would you handle this situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays calm and cooperative, identifies self and role, does not obstruct police or escalate the interaction
- Knows the limits of their authority: does not speak for the youth, supports the youth's right to have a guardian, social worker or lawyer involved
- Contacts the manager or on call and the MCFD social worker as soon as practical, and checks what information can be shared
- Stays with the youth where possible, explains what is happening in plain language, and helps them regulate
- Documents facts only, including officer names and file or badge numbers, times and what was said, and completes the incident report
- Debriefs with the youth afterward and with their own manager

questions.text: There are times when a youth may be very loud, verbally aggressive and inappropriate with staff. How would you respond in this situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Does not take it personally; reads the behaviour as communication or a trauma response rather than a challenge to authority
- Lowers voice and body language, gives space and time, reduces demands and audience, avoids arguing, ultimatums or power struggles
- Uses Mandt style de-escalation, offers simple choices, checks the individual support guidelines and safety or behaviour support plan for known triggers and strategies
- Monitors own regulation, and calls in a co worker or manager if they feel triggered or the situation is escalating
- Reconnects and repairs with the youth once calm, sets boundaries without shaming
- Documents the incident and shares patterns with the team so plans can be adjusted

questions.text: If you see a youth or others using drugs what would your response be?
questions.answerKey:
- Prioritises immediate safety of the youth, other people supported and self, and checks for signs of overdose
- Non judgemental, harm reduction stance: no lecturing or shaming, stays engaged so the youth does not use alone or hide it
- Removes other youth from the situation where needed, does not physically confront others who are using
- Notifies manager or on call, and the MCFD social worker; follows the critical or reportable incident process
- Knows where naloxone is and that it is accessible and in date
- Follows up later when the youth is regulated: curious conversation, connects to supports, documents facts without speculation

questions.text: If you saw a youth overdosing what would you do?
questions.answerKey:
- Recognises signs: unresponsive, slow or absent breathing, blue lips or fingertips, snoring or gurgling
- Calls 911, administers naloxone per training, gives rescue breaths or CPR, stays with the youth
- Repeats naloxone doses as needed and stays until paramedics arrive; keeps the youth in recovery position if breathing
- Notifies manager or on call and the social worker; treats as a critical or reportable incident with prompt documentation
- Supports other youth in the home who witnessed it, and seeks their own debrief afterward

questions.text: If the youth you are supporting is making threats towards you. What are you going to do?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays calm and does not respond to the threat with threats, punishment or a power struggle
- Assesses risk in the moment using something like RADAR: exit route, distance, whether the youth has a weapon or is escalating, whether to withdraw
- Gives space and time, drops non essential demands, keeps talking low and simple, calls for backup or on call if risk is rising
- Distinguishes venting from credible risk to safety and knows when to call police as a last resort
- Reports to manager, documents the incident factually, and follows up on the safety or behaviour support plan
- Names their own reaction and seeks debrief; returns to relationship and repair with the youth rather than holding it against them

questions.text: When you are faced with conflict, what is your typical response? Fight/Flight/ or freeze. Tell me what does that look like?
questions.answerKey:
- Answers honestly with a specific pattern rather than saying they never react
- Describes concrete signs in the body: raised voice, heart rate, going quiet, wanting to leave the room, jaw or shoulders tightening
- Names how they notice it early and what they do about it: breathing, stepping back, handing over to a co worker, taking a break after
- Shows the difference between their instinct and their practised response in shift
- Uses debriefs, supervision or team support rather than carrying it alone

questions.text: Have you ever been confronted by a person you have served? What does that look like?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a real, specific example with enough detail to judge, not a general statement
- Describes what they did in the moment: space, tone, avoiding cornering the person or arguing
- Names what they think set it off and what the behaviour was communicating
- Reports who they told and what was documented
- Describes repair afterward and whether the relationship recovered
- Reflects on their own regulation during and after

questions.text: Have you been surprised by your own reaction to a challenging situation? If yes, knowing what you know now, would you have done something different if this happened again?
questions.answerKey:
- Willing to name a moment where their reaction surprised them rather than presenting as always composed
- Specific about what the reaction was: froze, snapped, over involved, missed something, took it personally
- No blaming of the person supported for their own response
- Identifies clearly what they would do differently and why, including who they would loop in earlier
- Shows the learning changed their practice since, not just their intention

questions.text: Do you have anything else you would find relevant for us to know?
questions.answerKey:
- Note anything relevant to scheduling: availability, overnights, awake or asleep shifts, notice period, other employment
- Confirm driver's licence, driving record and comfort transporting youth in the community
- Note any certifications or training raised: first aid, naloxone, Mandt, food safe, non violent crisis intervention
- Note relevant experience or interests the candidate wants considered, and any questions they ask about the role or supports
- Follow up on anything the candidate raises that affects suitability or onboarding

questions.text: Scenario: You are on your way to the library with a youth you support to complete their homework. The youth suddenly changes their mind and now would like to go to the park where they have been in trouble in the past. What would you do and why?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays curious rather than saying no outright: asks what changed, what they want at the park, whether something about the library is hard today
- Balances self determination with the youth's plan and safety, and checks what the individual support guidelines or safety plan say about that location
- Offers real choices and negotiation: homework first then a different park, or a shorter visit with staff present
- Avoids a power struggle in the community; does not argue in public or make it a compliance battle
- Contacts the manager or on call if the youth insists and there is a genuine safety concern or a plan restriction
- Documents the change and any concerns, and raises the pattern with the team afterward

questions.text: Have you ever been involved in an MCFD protocol investigation or an internal agency investigation?
questions.answerKey:
- Straightforward yes or no; confirm whether it involved MCFD or an internal agency investigation
- If yes, note the general nature, the candidate's role in it and the outcome, without pressing for confidential detail
- Confirm they understood and cooperated with the process, including any temporary duty changes
- Note how they describe it: factual and non defensive, respectful of the person supported's privacy
- Note any learning or practice change they identify, and whether follow up with references is needed

questions.text: Why is documentation important? How do you think it is used in your role as a child and youth support worker?
questions.answerKey:
- Documentation is the record of what actually happened, written factually and objectively, separating observation from opinion or interpretation
- Written same shift while details are fresh, so the next staff coming on know what happened and support stays consistent across a single staffed home
- Tracks progress on ISP goals, patterns in behaviour, sleep, mood, medication including PRN given and its effect
- Feeds incident reporting at the right tier (general, critical, reportable) and supports duty to report, protocols and MCFD involvement
- Recognises it is a legal record that can be read by the youth, family, funders or in court, so language is respectful and non judgemental
- Knows what to escalate verbally to a manager rather than only writing it in a log

questions.text: Having a sense of belonging is so important for everyone. How could you help support a youth living in a residential home have a sense of belonging and feel safe?
questions.answerKey:
- Consistency and predictability: reliable routines, following through on what was promised, showing up the same way each shift
- Making the physical space theirs: personalising their bedroom, their food preferences, photos, belongings treated with respect
- Genuine interest in the youth as a person, their music, sport, humour, and building rapport in ordinary shared moments rather than formal talks
- Supporting connection outside the home: family where safe and appropriate, culture, community, school, friends, activities they choose
- Trauma informed framing: understanding testing behaviour as checking whether staff will stay, and responding without withdrawal or punishment
- Involving the youth in decisions about the home, house meetings, chores, meal planning, so they have a voice and self determination

questions.text: Scenario: A youth that was out arrives home yelling and becomes aggressive towards another youth in the home. The behavior continues to escalate. How would you respond?
questions.answerKey:
- First priority is safety of the other youth: separate the two, move the uninvolved youth to another space, reduce audience and stimulation
- Calm, low tone, non confrontational body language and space, no cornering, no matching the youth's volume or getting drawn into a power struggle
- Uses Mandt de-escalation, short simple words, gives time and choices, avoids demands and consequences in the moment; physical intervention only as a last resort if trained and there is imminent risk
- Checks the individual support guidelines and safety or behaviour support plan for known triggers and what works for this youth
- Calls for support: manager or on call, and police or emergency services if risk exceeds what one staff can safely manage
- Afterwards: check in with both youth separately, repair the relationship without lecturing, complete incident documentation and notify manager, and debrief own reaction and regulation

questions.text: F. Do you speak any other language, other than English, fluently?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm which languages and the level of fluency in speaking, reading and writing
- Note relevance to the people supported and families served in the program
- No scoring beyond recording the information for staffing and matching purposes

questions.text: How would you help support an Indigenous youth connect to their home community?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts by asking the youth what connection they want, at their pace, rather than assuming or imposing
- Works with the youth's ISP, MCFD worker, band or Nation representative, family and any cultural plan already in place
- Practical supports: transport to community events, powwows, feasts, ceremony, contact with extended family, band office, Elders
- Brings culture into daily life at the home: food, language, music, art, materials and books, honouring what the youth identifies with rather than a generic pan Indigenous version
- Recognises the impact of residential schools and the child welfare system, and that hesitation or anger about identity is understandable
- Knows own limits as a non Indigenous staff member if applicable, seeks guidance rather than positioning self as the cultural teacher

questions.text: Give us an example of how you have encouraged and supported a youth that was hesitant to explore their cultural background become connected with their heritage?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific example from their own experience with a real youth, not a general statement of values
- Followed the youth's pace and interest, offering low pressure openings such as food, music, art or an event rather than pushing
- Explored the reason for the hesitation without judgement, which may include shame, grief, fear of not belonging or family disconnection
- Brought in the right people: family, community members, Elders, cultural workers, rather than doing it alone
- Describes the outcome honestly, including partial or slow progress, and what they would do differently

questions.text: What are some ways you could support a youth to increase their independence?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts from the youth's own goals in the ISP and what independence means to them, not staff's idea of what they should be doing
- Teaches practical life skills alongside them: cooking, laundry, budgeting, cleaning, bus routes, appointments, ID and documents, banking
- Steps back gradually, coaching and prompting rather than doing it for them, allowing dignity of risk and room to make mistakes safely
- Uses natural daily opportunities rather than formal lessons, and repeats skills patiently without shaming errors
- Builds self advocacy: speaking up at school, medical appointments, with their MCFD worker
- Links to transition to adulthood planning and community supports before the youth ages out

questions.text: What do you think is appropriate work attire when working with youth? (ensure they understand modesty and dressing conservatively)
questions.answerKey:
- Modest and conservative: no low cut, cropped, sheer or revealing clothing, nothing with offensive or drug and alcohol related slogans
- Practical and safe for the work: closed toe shoes, clothing you can move, run or do a physical intervention in, minimal jewellery
- Clean, neat and casual rather than formal, so the home feels like a home and the youth are not embarrassed by staff appearance
- Understands the boundary reason: attire that is respectful of youth who may have trauma histories and avoids any sexualised or ambiguous message
- Adjusts to the activity and setting, for example swimming, outings, or community appointments

questions.text: As you know this type of work can be stressful, what do you do outside of work to relax or destress?
questions.answerKey:
- Names specific, realistic strategies they actually use, such as exercise, time outdoors, family or friends, hobbies, faith, rest, counselling
- Shows awareness of their own early warning signs of stress and compassion fatigue and what they do when they notice them
- Separates work from home: not taking shifts home, using debriefs with a manager or team after difficult incidents
- Understands that self regulation directly affects their ability to de-escalate and stay present with youth
- Recognises when to ask for support rather than pushing through, including after a critical incident or protocol

questions.text: Do you have any conditions, situations and/or pre-existing injuries that would impact your ability to do the job?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can perform the physical requirements of the role, including Mandt physical intervention, lifting, standing and driving as required
- Note any accommodation the candidate raises and follow up on it separately through the appropriate process
- Confirm ability to work the shift pattern for the position, including awake overnight, sleep shifts and single staffed shifts
- Record the answer factually only; no scoring or further probing into medical detail

name: Children and Family Services, External
description: External applicants to Milieu Children and Family Services.

questions.text: Do you have a BC Class 5 Driver License? YES / NO (7N may be considered); Driving is a requirement of the job; are you willing to do so YES /
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms a valid BC Class 5 (or 7N, which may be considered) and notes any restrictions
- Confirms willingness to drive as part of the role, including transporting youth in the community
- Note access to a vehicle, insurance status, and comfort driving in the Lower Mainland
- Flag for follow up: driver's abstract, licence class verification, any pending items

questions.text: Do you have any commitments (school, vacation, travel) that would affect your availability over the next 3-6 months?
questions.answerKey:
- States any school, vacation or travel commitments with approximate dates
- Confirms availability against the shifts the posting requires, including evenings, weekends, overnights or single staffed shifts
- Notes earliest possible start date and any notice period with a current employer
- Flag for follow up: conflicts with training dates or scheduling blocks

questions.text: Have you lived in another provinces besides BC? If yes, where?
questions.answerKey:
- Yes or no, with the province or provinces named
- Approximate dates of residence in each
- Note for follow up: out of province criminal record and prior contact checks may be required
