questions.text: Have you lived outside of Canada for longer than 6 months since the age of 18? If yes, where?
questions.answerKey:
- Yes or no, with the country or countries named
- Approximate dates of residence since age 18
- Note for follow up: international police clearance or additional screening may be required before hire

questions.text: What skills, experience and education do you have that make you an ideal candidate for this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Names relevant education or training (child and youth care, social work, human services, trauma informed practice, Mandt, first aid, Narcan) and how it applies day to day
- Gives concrete experience with children, youth or families, including residential, respite, school or community settings
- Describes practical skills the role needs: de-escalation, documentation and incident reporting, daily living and routine support, working alone on shift
- Connects skills to person centred, trauma informed support rather than listing credentials
- Shows self awareness about what they are still learning and where they would seek supervision

questions.text: Tell us about your approach to caregiving i.e. Communication style, conflict resolution skills, appropriate discipline techniques?
questions.answerKey:
- Communication that is calm, clear and respectful, with listening and giving youth real choice and voice
- Conflict resolution that avoids power struggles: lowering demands in the moment, offering space and time, revisiting once everyone is regulated
- Understands discipline as teaching and natural or logical consequences within the person's plan, never physical, shaming or withholding of basics
- References individual support guidelines, safety or behaviour support plans and consistency with the team
- Names own triggers and regulation strategies, and when to hand off to a co-worker or call the manager
- Follows up with documentation and debrief after significant incidents

questions.text: The youth we support come into our services for various reasons, what do you think are some of the challenges and barriers that may have contributed to the youth needing services? What would be helpful?
questions.answerKey:
- Identifies barriers such as trauma, family breakdown, abuse or neglect, attachment disruption, multiple placements, poverty and unstable housing
- Mentions substance use, mental health, FASD or developmental diversabilities, school disengagement, systemic and cultural barriers including Indigenous youth in care
- Frames behaviour as a response to unmet need and past experience rather than as a character issue
- What helps: consistent and predictable relationships, routine, patience over time, unconditional regard when a youth tests the relationship
- What helps: connection to family, culture and community, school and employment supports, coordinated work with MCFD, schools and other professionals
- Practical supports such as life skills, transition to adulthood planning and advocating for the youth's own goals

questions.text: Which value resonates with you the most? Please give us an example from your current position of how your values align with Milieu's
questions.answerKey:
- Names one of Milieu's values (integrity, accountability, self-determination, person-centred, inclusiveness, respect) rather than a general statement
- Explains in their own words what that value looks like in day to day practice
- Gives a real example from current or recent work, with what they actually did
- Example shows the person supported having choice, dignity or voice, not just staff efficiency
- Includes accountability: owning a mistake, reporting something, or raising a concern when it would have been easier not to

questions.text: At Milieu, we have a goal setting process for each supported person called an Individual Support Plan. Describe a situation in which you supported a person to set a meaningful goal and the steps they took to achieve it?
questions.answerKey:
- The goal came from the person supported, in their words, not from staff or family preference
- Describes breaking the goal into achievable steps with realistic timelines
- Describes their own supporting role: teaching, prompting, transport, connecting to community resources, stepping back as skills grow
- Notes progress tracking and documentation, and reviewing or adjusting the goal when it was not working
- Acknowledges setbacks or a goal not fully met, and how they kept the person's motivation and dignity intact
- Mentions the team, family and other professionals being kept informed and consistent

questions.text: Scenario: You are on your way to the library with a youth you support to complete their homework. The youth suddenly change their mind and now would like to go to the park where they have been in trouble in the past. What would you do and why?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays curious and asks what is behind the change of mind rather than refusing outright
- Checks the youth's individual support guidelines, safety plan and any conditions before agreeing to a location with known risk
- Avoids a power struggle in the car or on the street: calm tone, offers alternatives, negotiates the homework and a different location or a later time
- Names honestly what the concern is about the park and involves the youth in problem solving rather than lecturing
- Knows when to call the manager or on-call for direction, particularly if there are conditions, safety concerns or the youth leaves
- Documents the change of plan and what was discussed, and debriefs with the team so the response is consistent next time

questions.text: Scenario: While on the bus to an activity, the individual you are supporting hits a fellow passenger. How would you respond?
questions.answerKey:
- Immediate safety first: places themselves between the person supported and the passenger, gets space, requests the driver stop and exits the bus at the next safe opportunity
- Checks on the passenger, apologises without disclosing confidential information about the person supported, offers to exchange information if police or the transit operator require it
- De-escalates the person supported calmly, using low demands and their known plan, rather than confronting or restraining unless there is imminent risk and Mandt trained intervention is required
- Considers what triggered the incident, crowding, noise, sensory load, and adjusts the plan for getting home
- Notifies the manager or on-call promptly and completes incident documentation at the appropriate tier, critical or reportable as applicable
- Follows up: debrief with the person supported when regulated, team debrief, review of guidelines or travel plan, and attention to their own regulation after the event

questions.text: Please give example of something you have done to be a good team member or to improve teamwork?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific example, not a general statement about being a team player
- Shows reliability: thorough shift handovers, accurate logs, covering shifts, following through on what was agreed
- Describes consistency across the team so people supported get the same approach from everyone
- Raises a disagreement or concern directly and respectfully, and takes it to the manager when needed rather than talking around a co-worker
- Supports newer staff, shares knowledge, or checks in on a co-worker after a difficult incident
- Reflects on their own part when the team dynamic was strained and what they changed

questions.text: Describe a situation where you had conflict with your supervisor or a co-worker?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a real, specific example rather than saying they have never had conflict
- Describes going directly to the person first, in private and at a calm time, rather than venting to other staff or in front of youth
- Separates the issue from the person, stays focused on practice and impact on the people supported
- Shows willingness to escalate to a supervisor or follow the chain of command if it stayed unresolved
- Reflects on their own contribution and what they would do differently, and on how they regulated themselves in the moment

questions.text: What is professional confidentiality?
questions.answerKey:
- Information about a person supported and their family is shared only with those who need it to provide support
- No discussion of youth in public places, with friends or family, or on social media, and no photos or identifying details posted
- Records, notes and devices kept secure, files not taken home or left accessible
- Understands confidentiality is not absolute: duty to report suspected abuse or neglect, and risk of harm to self or others, override it
- Mentions telling the youth up front what they can and cannot keep private rather than promising secrecy

questions.text: Please describe the rights of children and youth in care?
questions.answerKey:
- To be safe, and to be free from abuse, neglect and physical punishment
- To be treated with respect and dignity, and to have their culture, language, spirituality, race, gender identity and sexual orientation respected
- To privacy, to their own belongings, and to private communication with family, social worker, lawyer or advocate
- To be informed and to have a say in decisions and plans that affect them, including their care plan
- To food, clothing, education, health care and recreation, and to contact with family and community where appropriate
- To be told their rights in a way they understand, and to complain or contact an advocate without fear of consequences

questions.text: If you witnessed something that breeched our policies or rights of children in care, what would you do? (looking to see if they know procedure for Duty to Report)
questions.answerKey:
- Acts immediately to make sure the youth is safe and the behaviour stops
- Reports to the manager or on call right away, and documents factually and promptly
- Knows duty to report is personal and legal: if abuse or neglect is suspected they report to MCFD themselves and do not rely on someone else doing it
- Understands they cannot be talked out of reporting by a co-worker or supervisor, and that reporting is not conditional on being certain
- Records only what was seen and heard, without adding opinion or investigating on their own
- Cooperates with any protocol or investigation that follows

questions.text: Tell us about your experience working with people who sometimes communicate using challenging behaviour. What did it look like? What do you think the person was trying to communicate?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete example with real detail about what the behaviour looked like, not a general statement
- Frames the behaviour as communication and looks for the unmet need behind it: fear, pain, overwhelm, hunger, wanting control or connection, trauma reminder
- Notes what came before it, environment, time of day, who was present, what was being asked of the person
- Describes how they responded in the moment: lowered demands, gave space and time, calm tone, avoided a power struggle
- Shows awareness of their own reaction and how they stayed regulated

questions.text: What could have been done to support this person to get their needs met without having them use challenging behaviour? (HR - Give Details)
questions.answerKey:
- Identifies specific antecedents or triggers that could have been changed, such as pacing, noise, transitions, or how the request was made
- Building relationship and predictability so the person does not have to escalate to be heard
- Offering real choice and control earlier, and teaching or accepting another way to communicate the same need
- Using what is known about the person from their support plan, guidelines and the people who know them best
- Recognises the person may not have had another way available to them, and avoids blaming
- Bringing it back to the team, documenting patterns, and raising suggested changes with the manager

questions.text: If a youth were to come to you and disclose their history or experience of abuse and or trauma. How would you respond to this disclosure?
questions.answerKey:
- Stops, gives full attention, stays calm and does not react with visible shock or judgement
- Listens and lets the youth lead, does not probe for details, does not ask leading or investigative questions
- Believes and validates: thanks them for telling, tells them it is not their fault
- Does not promise to keep it secret, explains honestly what they have to do next and who they have to tell
- Reports to the manager and follows duty to report to MCFD, documents the youth's own words as soon as possible
- Checks in with the youth afterward, keeps routine and support normal, and seeks their own debrief and support

questions.text: If the youth you are working with comes to you and tell you they have been sexually assaulted or abused by someone? What would you do and how would you respond to this situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Responds calmly, listens without pressing for detail, and takes the disclosure seriously
- Makes sure the youth is safe now and there is no ongoing contact with the person named
- Attends to immediate medical need if the assault is recent, and considers police or hospital involvement without pressuring the youth
- Does not promise confidentiality, explains what happens next in plain language, and keeps the youth informed
- Reports to MCFD under duty to report and notifies the manager or on call immediately, without waiting
- Documents the youth's exact words and the facts only, does not investigate or contact the alleged person
- Follows up with the youth and accesses their own debriefing support

questions.text: In your role as a staff, you may experience the youth using racial slurs towards you. How would you cope with this scenario?
questions.answerKey:
- Does not take it personally in the moment, stays regulated, avoids arguing or retaliating
- Keeps the immediate focus on de-escalation and safety rather than winning the point
- Names the impact simply and clearly at a calm time later, and sets a boundary without shaming the youth
- Considers what the youth was trying to communicate or push away, and whether they were testing whether staff will leave
- Honest that it affects them, and will debrief with the manager and team rather than carrying it alone
- Documents the incident and raises it with the team so there is a consistent approach

questions.text: If a youth is talking to you about killing themselves, how would you handle this situation? And would you do anything different if they actually attempted to kill themselves?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays with the youth, takes it seriously every time, and does not minimise or leave them alone
- Asks directly and calmly about plan, means and timeframe, and listens without judgement
- Removes or reduces access to means, and does not agree to keep it secret
- Notifies the manager or on call immediately, follows the youth's safety plan, and involves crisis line, social worker or hospital as indicated
- If an attempt has occurred: calls 911 and gives first aid at once, this becomes a critical or reportable incident, and reporting and documentation happen immediately rather than at end of shift
- Documents factually, supports the youth afterward without shaming, and seeks their own debrief

questions.text: How would you respond to witnessing a youth self-harming or displaying self-injurious behavior (e.g., cutting or hitting their head against the wall)?
questions.answerKey:
- Responds calmly and without shock, shame or ultimatums, keeps their own reaction contained
- Attends to immediate safety and first aid, and seeks medical attention for the injury when needed
- Reduces access to means where possible and stays present, uses a low demand, low stimulation approach rather than force
- Follows the youth's safety or behaviour support plan and their individual support guidelines
- Understands self harm often serves a coping or regulating function, and follows up later about what was going on and what else could help
- Notifies the manager, documents the incident factually, and follows the incident reporting process

questions.text: If you had to take a youth to the hospital for any reason would you be okay with supporting the youth in the hospital?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm a clear yes, including comfort with long waits in emergency and staying for the duration of the shift
- Confirm willingness to stay with the youth, advocate for them and communicate with hospital staff
- Confirm they would notify the manager or on call and complete the required incident documentation
- Note any limits raised, such as transport arrangements or use of own vehicle, for follow up

questions.text: There are times you will have to deal with police interactions regarding the youth you are supporting. If this was the case, how would you handle this situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays calm and present, does not take over or obstruct, and remains a support to the youth rather than acting as an investigator or enforcer
- Knows their role: identify themselves as staff, provide factual information about the youth's care, and avoid speculating or sharing more personal information than needed
- Contacts the manager on call early, and understands the social worker or guardian may need to be involved for interviews or statements involving a youth in care
- Debriefs with the youth afterward without shaming, and supports them through the aftermath (charges, conditions, curfew, court dates)
- Documents the interaction factually and follows incident reporting, treating a police attendance as a critical or reportable incident depending on what occurred
- Gives a concrete example of past police contact and how they kept the relationship with the young person intact

questions.text: There are times when a youth may be very loud, verbally aggressive and inappropriate with staff. How would you respond in this situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Does not take the words personally, recognises escalation as communication of distress or unmet need rather than an attack on them
- Lowers voice and stimulation, gives space and time, drops non essential demands, avoids arguing, correcting or issuing ultimatums that create a power struggle
- Monitors their own regulation, uses another staff member to take over if they are becoming activated
- Attends to safety of the youth, other people supported and themselves; knows Mandt de-escalation and that physical intervention is a last resort
- Circles back once the youth is regulated to repair the relationship and problem solve, rather than at the peak of the incident
- Follows the youth's individual support guidelines or safety plan, documents, and reports to the manager

questions.text: If you see a youth or others using drugs what would your response be?
questions.answerKey:
- Prioritises immediate safety and health over confrontation; does not physically grab or wrestle for substances
- Responds without judgement or lecturing, uses a harm reduction lens and keeps the relationship open so the youth will tell them next time
- Checks what was used and how much, watches for signs of overdose, ensures naloxone is accessible
- Asks others not connected to the program to leave the home or area, and calls for support or police if there is a safety risk they cannot manage alone
- Notifies the manager on call, documents factually, and completes the appropriate incident report
- Follows up later when the youth is regulated: talks about safety, supplies, and connects to resources per their plan

questions.text: If you saw a youth overdosing what would you do?
questions.answerKey:
- Checks responsiveness and breathing, calls 911 immediately, and does not leave the youth alone
- Administers naloxone per training, gives rescue breaths or CPR as indicated, stays with them and gives repeat doses if breathing does not return
- Places in recovery position once breathing and stays until ambulance arrives; understands the effect can wear off and they can re-enter overdose
- Notes what was taken and when if known, and passes that to paramedics
- Notifies manager on call, completes a critical or reportable incident report, and notifies the social worker or guardian
- Seeks their own debrief afterward and recognises the impact of the event on other youth in the home

questions.text: If the youth you are supporting is making threats towards you. What are you going to do?
questions.answerKey:
- Distinguishes between venting or testing and a credible threat with intent and means, and responds proportionately
- Keeps voice low, gives space, does not escalate with threats of consequences or by cornering the youth; positions themselves near an exit
- Uses RADAR style thinking: recognise the risk, assess, decide, act, review; removes themselves or others if the situation is not safe
- Calls the manager on call, and police if there is immediate danger they cannot manage
- Does not carry it as a personal grievance; returns to the relationship when the youth is regulated and works on repair
- Documents the threat in specific factual language, completes an incident report, and asks for a debrief and any update to the safety plan

questions.text: When you are faced with conflict, what is your typical response? Fight/Flight/ or freeze. Tell me what does that look like?
questions.answerKey:
- Answers honestly with a real self assessment rather than an idealised one
- Describes concrete physical and behavioural signs (raised voice, going quiet, tightening up, wanting to leave the room, going into problem solving)
- Shows awareness of how that tendency helps or hinders when supporting a youth in crisis
- Names specific strategies they use to regulate: breathing, stepping out, tagging in another staff, delaying the conversation
- Mentions using supervision, debriefing and team support rather than managing it alone

questions.text: Have you ever been confronted by a person you have served? What does that look like?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific example with enough detail to judge, not a general statement
- Describes what the confrontation was actually about and what the person may have been communicating
- Shows they held boundaries without escalating or retaliating, and did not make it a contest
- Describes what they did afterward: repair with the person supported, documentation, reporting to a manager
- Reflects on their own reaction and regulation during and after the incident

questions.text: Have you been surprised by your own reaction to a challenging situation? If yes, knowing what you know now, would you have done something different if this happened again?
questions.answerKey:
- Willing to name a real moment where their reaction surprised them rather than deflecting
- Describes the reaction specifically and without excessive self criticism or blame of the person supported
- Identifies what they now understand about the trigger, their own history, or what they missed in the moment
- States a concrete change in practice: seeking support earlier, stepping back, asking a colleague to take over, debriefing
- Shows they used supervision, debriefing or training to work it through rather than absorbing it alone

questions.text: Do you have anything else you would find relevant for us to know?
questions.answerKey:
- Raises anything relevant to suitability: relevant training (Mandt, naloxone, first aid, non violent crisis intervention), driver's licence, criminal record check status
- Notes availability, shift preferences, capacity for awake overnight, evening or single staffed shifts
- Mentions any conditions, restrictions or scheduling constraints the interviewer needs to follow up on
- Adds relevant lived or work experience not yet covered, or asks informed questions about the program and supports available to staff

questions.text: Have you ever been involved in an MCFD protocol investigation or an internal agency investigation?
questions.answerKey:
- Answers directly yes or no; if yes, describes their role (subject, witness, reporter) and the outcome at a factual level
- Speaks about it without breaching confidentiality of the youth or other staff involved
- Shows understanding that an investigation is a normal accountability process and that cooperating fully is expected
- Describes how they conducted themselves during it: honest account, accurate documentation, following direction from the manager, not discussing it with others
- Reflects on what changed in their practice afterward
- Interviewer to note any outstanding or unresolved matters for follow up

questions.text: Why is documentation important? How do you think it is used in your role as a child and youth support worker?
questions.answerKey:
- Documentation is the record of the youth's care and continuity between shifts, especially in single staffed homes where staff do not overlap
- Written objectively and factually: what was observed and said, not opinion, diagnosis or assumption
- Written promptly and completed before the end of shift while the detail is accurate
- Used by the team, manager, social worker, MCFD and funders, and can be read in a protocol investigation, court proceeding or file review
- Tracks patterns over time so triggers, progress toward ISP goals and changes in presentation can be seen
- Distinguishes daily logs from incident reporting and knows general, critical and reportable incidents each have their own process
- Handled confidentially and stored as required

questions.text: What do you think is appropriate work attire when working with youth? (ensure they understand modesty and dressing conservatively)
questions.answerKey:
- Modest and conservative: no low cut, cropped, sheer or revealing clothing, nothing with offensive or drug and alcohol related images or slogans
- Practical for the work: clean, comfortable, closed toe shoes, able to move quickly, do personal care, drive, cook, be outdoors and respond to a physical incident
- Understands the reason is professional boundaries and the vulnerability and trauma histories of the youth, not just appearance
- Limits expensive items, excessive jewellery and anything that could be grabbed during an escalation
- Recognises staff model appropriate presentation for youth, and that they are in a workplace even though it is someone's home
- Willing to follow program specific direction and adjust if asked

questions.text: Milieu has a zero tolerance for abuse policy. Can you list actions that would constitute abuse?
questions.answerKey:
- Names physical abuse: hitting, rough handling, unnecessary or improper physical restraint
- Names emotional and verbal abuse: yelling, name calling, threats, humiliation, isolating a youth, withholding affection or contact
- Names sexual abuse and any sexualised comment, contact or boundary breach
- Names financial abuse: taking or misusing a youth's money, allowance or belongings
- Names neglect: withholding food, medication, clothing, medical care, supervision or emotional support
- Recognises subtler forms such as withholding privileges as punishment, ignoring a youth, breaching privacy, or misuse of staff power and position

questions.text: How would you respond if you saw your co-worker abuse an individual in any way? (Briefly explain reporting procedure to the applicant)
questions.answerKey:
- Acts immediately to make the person supported safe and interrupts the situation without escalating into a confrontation in front of the youth
- States clearly they would report and would never keep it quiet or handle it privately with the co-worker, regardless of friendship or seniority
- Reports to the manager or on call right away, and knows the duty to report means notifying MCFD directly and independent of internal reporting
- Documents factually and promptly: what was seen and heard, times, who was present, no opinion or speculation
- Understands this is a reportable incident and that a protocol or investigation may follow, and cooperates with it
- Checks in with the youth afterwards and supports them without leading or questioning them investigatively

questions.text: Having a sense of belonging is so important for everyone. How could you help support a youth living in a residential home have a sense of belonging and feel safe?
questions.answerKey:
- Builds relationship first: consistent presence, following through on what is promised, one to one time doing what the youth actually likes
- Helps the youth make the space their own: bedroom decoration, personal belongings, food they like, choice in routines and meals
- Involves the youth in decisions about the home rather than presenting rules as fixed, and treats house meetings and choices as genuine
- Supports connection outside the home: family, siblings, culture and community, friends, school, sports or hobbies
- Creates safety through predictability: clear routines, warning about changes, calm consistent responses when the youth tests the relationship
- Recognises trauma and attachment history means trust takes time, and does not take rejection or testing personally

questions.text: As you know this type of work can be stressful, what do you do outside of work to relax or destress?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives concrete specific activities they actually do rather than a general statement about self care
- Shows awareness of their own early warning signs of stress or burnout
- Describes separating work from home life, including not carrying shifts home or contacting youth off shift
- Uses supports appropriately: debriefing with a supervisor or team after a hard shift, employee supports, own counselling or peer support
- Connects regulation to practice: recognises that their own state affects how they respond to a youth in crisis and knows when to step back and let a co-worker take over

questions.text: Scenario: A youth that was out arrives home yelling and becomes aggressive towards another youth in the home. The behaviour continues to escalate. How would you respond?
questions.answerKey:
- Prioritises safety of the other youth first: separates the two, moves the other youth to another room or space, considers others present in the home
- Approaches the escalated youth calmly, gives space and time, lowers voice, avoids cornering, avoids demands, ultimatums and power struggles
- Uses de-escalation consistent with Mandt, with physical intervention only as a last resort when there is risk of harm and only as trained
- Checks the youth's individual support guidelines, safety plan or behaviour support plan and known triggers and calming strategies
- Knows when to call for backup: on call or manager, and police only if safety cannot be maintained
- After the incident: debriefs with both youth when they are regulated, repairs the relationship without shaming, documents as a critical or reportable incident as required, and notifies the manager

questions.text: What experience do you have giving medications? What would you do if a youth refused their medication?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes actual experience: setting, blister packs or bubble packs, PRN medication, documenting administration, following training and certification
- Follows the basic checks: right person, right medication, right dose, right time, and signs the record immediately
- Treats refusal as a right, does not force, bribe, threaten or hide medication in food
- Explores the refusal: asks what is going on, side effects, timing, offers again later, gives choice about how and when where possible
- Documents the refusal and notifies the manager or on call, and follows up with the pharmacy, prescriber or nurse where the medication is time sensitive or missed doses matter
- Knows to escalate immediately if the refusal or a medication error creates a health risk

questions.text: Have you provided personal care? If yes, in what capacity? If no, are you willing to do it with proper training?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm whether they have provided personal care and in what setting and role
- If experienced: examples such as bathing, toileting, dressing, feeding, transfers, incontinence care
- Attention to dignity and privacy: explaining before doing, offering choice, same gender preferences, maintaining the person's routine and pace
- If no experience: clear willingness to do it and to complete training before providing care
- Follow up on any limits or conditions the candidate names

questions.text: Have you supported people with medical related needs? If so, please detail experience
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the type of medical needs supported: seizures, diabetes, G tube, mobility and lifts, mental health, substance use, complex health conditions
- Describes following care plans and health protocols, and recording and reporting changes in condition
- Comfort recognising when something is outside their scope and contacting the manager, nurse line, 811 or emergency services
- Overdose response relevant to youth work: naloxone or Narcan training and willingness to be trained
- Willingness to complete required training for specific health tasks before performing them

questions.text: Do you speak any other language, other than English, fluently? -
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm which languages and the level of fluency in speaking, reading and writing
- Note any languages relevant to people currently supported or to the local community
- Note if they have used the language in a work or interpreting capacity
- Record for staffing and matching purposes only, no scoring

questions.text: How would you help support an Indigenous youth connect to their home community?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts by asking the youth what connection they want and follows their pace, rather than assuming or imposing
- Works with the youth's family, extended family, band or Nation, and the MCFD social worker to identify the home community and any existing contacts
- Makes it practical: transport to community events, powwows, feasts, cultural camps, connecting with an Elder or cultural worker, helping the youth research their Nation
- Builds culture into daily life at the home: food, language, music, art, medicines, ceremony, and marking days that matter to the youth
- Names the impact of residential schools and the child welfare system, approaches with humility, and does not position themselves as the cultural expert
- Records the connection goals in the ISP and follows through consistently rather than as a one off event

questions.text: Give us an example of how you have encouraged and supported a youth that was hesitant to explore their cultural background become connected with their heritage?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific real example with the youth's hesitation named and what was actually done
- Explored the reason for the hesitation: shame, fear of rejection, past experience, mixed family messages, not knowing enough to start
- Offered low pressure entry points such as food, music, film, art or a community event rather than a formal program
- Followed the youth's lead and accepted a no without pushing, leaving the door open
- Involved family, community members or cultural workers rather than doing it alone
- Describes the outcome honestly, including where progress was partial or slow

questions.text: What are some ways you could support a youth to increase their independence?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts from what the youth wants and what matters to them, tied to their ISP goals, rather than a staff checklist
- Teaches concrete daily living skills alongside the youth: cooking, laundry, budgeting, shopping, transit, appointments, banking, ID and documents
- Uses gradual release: do it together, then prompt, then step back, and expects setbacks without taking over
- Builds decision making and self advocacy: letting the youth speak for themselves at appointments and in meetings, and allowing safe mistakes with natural consequences
- Connects the youth to community outside the home: school, work, volunteering, recreation, and their own supports for after they leave care
- Recognises transition to adulthood needs planning well in advance and works with the social worker and family on it

questions.text: Do you have any conditions, situations and/or pre-existing injuries that would impact your ability to do the job? (Yes or No answers only)
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes or no answer; no medical detail sought or recorded
- If yes, note only that accommodation needs to be discussed and refer to the hiring manager or HR for follow up
- Confirm the candidate understands the physical and practical demands described (single staffed shifts, awake or overnight hours, driving, Mandt physical intervention, personal care where applicable)
- Record the answer as given and flag any follow up required before an offer

questions.text: Once you are hired, you would be orientated to several of the programs in your region. If there are imminent need in other houses, you may be asked to work there for your shift instead of the house in your line. Would you accept this job expectation? (Yes or No)
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes, understanding shifts may be redirected to another home in the region on short notice
- Confirms willingness to be orientated to several programs and to work across youth and adult settings as needed
- Confirms reliable transportation and travel time to other sites in the region
- If any limits (geography, hours, days), note them specifically for scheduling follow up
- A hesitant or conditional answer is noted as is, not scored as a behavioural response

questions.text: (If appropriate, say the following): Based on the Interview, are you still interested in this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes or no after hearing the shift pattern, program type and expectations
- Any conditions the candidate names (hours, start date, other employment, on call limits) recorded for follow up
- If still interested, confirm availability and earliest start date
- If not interested or unsure, note the reason briefly and close the file respectfully

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?
questions.answerKey:
- Questions show they have thought about the actual work: staffing ratios, single staffing, who the shift supports, behaviour and safety plans, on call and manager backup
- Asks about training and onboarding (Mandt, first aid, naloxone, medication, shadow shifts) and supervision or debriefing after difficult incidents
- Asks practical employment questions: scheduling, casual to regular lines, probation, pay, references and screening timelines
- No questions is acceptable if they have already covered their questions earlier; note any that require a follow up answer from the hiring manager

questions.text: The following items would be required for hire, do you currently have any of the following certificates or trainings?
questions.answerKey:
- States clearly which items are current, which are expired and which are not yet held, with expiry dates where known
- Standard items to confirm: Criminal Record Check for working with children and vulnerable adults, valid Class 5 BC driver's licence and driver's abstract, vehicle and business use insurance, first aid and CPR, Mandt, food safe, naloxone, medication administration, and any relevant education or credential
- Confirms willingness to obtain or renew outstanding items within the required timeframe and before starting shifts
- Confirms ability to provide employment references and copies of certificates
- Note any gaps for HR follow up rather than assessing them in the interview

questions.text: Do you have any conditions or previous injuries that might impact your ability to perform this role?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can meet the physical demands of the role: transfers, lifting, personal care, driving, awake or overnight shifts, Mandt physical intervention
- Note any disclosed injury or condition and whether accommodation is being requested, without probing for diagnosis or medical detail
- Follow up on what supports or modifications would be needed, and route any accommodation request to HR
- Confirm willingness and fitness to complete required training such as Mandt and first aid

questions.text: Do you have any commitments (school, vacation, travel, etc.) that might affect your availability in the next 3-6 months? List here
questions.answerKey:
- Specific dates and duration of any school terms, planned travel, vacation or other employment
- Class or shift conflicts that would limit availability, including weekends, evenings, awake overnights and on call
- Whether the candidate can commit to the full paid orientation and training schedule
- Notice already given or expected for other commitments, and any second job that affects rest between shifts

questions.text: Are there any barriers to you being able to provide personal care? (Explain that personal care is a requirement for this role.)
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms clearly that they can provide personal care after hearing what it involves: bathing, toileting, incontinence care, feeding, dressing, menstrual care
- No barrier related to gender of the person supported, bodily fluids, or cultural or personal discomfort, or names the limit honestly
- Prior experience providing personal care, or realistic understanding of what it will be like if new to it
- Talks about dignity and privacy during care: explaining what is happening, offering choice, closing doors, following the person's routine and preferences

questions.text: From the values outlined, which resonates with you the most, and why?Values
questions.answerKey:
- Names a specific value (integrity, accountability, self-determination, person-centred, inclusiveness, respect) rather than listing all of them
- Explains what that value looks like in daily shift work, not just what the word means
- Backs it with a concrete example from their own practice or life
- Connects the value to the person supported having control over their own life and being part of their community

questions.text: Professional Confidentiality: What does professional confidentiality mean to you?
questions.answerKey:
- Information about a person supported is shared only with people who need it to do their job, not with family, friends, roommates or other staff who are not involved
- Includes the person's health, behaviour, family situation, finances and history, and applies after employment ends
- No discussion in public places, in front of other people supported, or on social media, and no photos or identifying details posted
- Records, phones and files are kept secure; documentation stays in the agency system
- Recognises confidentiality has limits and is not the same as keeping secrets

questions.text: Can you provide an example of a situation where confidentiality would not apply
questions.answerKey:
- Duty to report: suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a child, youth or vulnerable adult must be reported regardless of who asks them to keep it quiet
- Risk of harm to self or others, including suicidal statements or a serious threat, is shared immediately with the manager and appropriate authorities
- Critical or reportable incidents, medication errors, allegations against staff, and information required for a protocol investigation
- Information shared with the team, manager or funder (MCFD, CLBC) so the person can be supported safely
- Does not promise a person supported that a disclosure will be kept secret; tells them up front what will have to be passed on

questions.text: How would you respond?
questions.answerKey:
- Stays calm and listens without interrogating, leading or asking probing investigative questions
- Tells the person honestly what will happen next and does not promise to keep it to themselves
- Attends to immediate safety first, then reports to the manager right away and makes the external report where duty to report applies
- Documents factually and promptly, in the person's own words where possible, separating observation from opinion
- Follows through: checks the report was made, does not discuss it beyond those who need to know, and seeks debrief or support for themselves

questions.text: Supervisor Feedback: If we asked your current or previous supervisor to describe you in two words, what would they say?
questions.answerKey:
- Two words that are specific and plausible, with a short example that shows where they come from
- Words that connect to the work: reliable, calm, teachable, consistent, follows through
- Some self awareness, including honesty about an area a supervisor would say they are still developing
- Answer suggests the supervisor is a reference the candidate is comfortable having contacted

questions.text: Conflict Resolution: Describe a situation where you had a conflict with your supervisor. How did you handle it, and what was the result?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a real, specific disagreement rather than saying they have never had one
- Raised it directly and privately with the supervisor rather than venting to co-workers or to people supported
- Separated the issue from the person, listened to the supervisor's reasoning, and stayed regulated
- Followed the direction given once the decision was made, or escalated appropriately if it involved safety or a reporting obligation
- Names the outcome honestly, including what they would do differently and what they learned

questions.text: Supporting Choices: How would you support a person with a developmental disability in making choices?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts from the person: their Individual Support Plan, goals, communication style and known preferences
- Offers real, limited choices in a form the person can use: objects, pictures, gestures, showing options, allowing time to respond
- Reads and honours non verbal communication and refusal as a valid answer
- Provides enough information about consequences so the choice is informed, without steering the person to the staff's preferred option
- Supports dignity of risk within the person's safety plan, and brings bigger decisions to the team, family or manager rather than deciding alone
- Recognises their own influence and avoids using the relationship or routine to pressure the person

questions.text: Mission Statement: Milieu's mission is "Supporting people to be valued, contributing citizens in communities." In your own words, what does this mean to you?
questions.answerKey:
- Puts it in their own words: people supported belong in the community, not apart from it
- Value and contribution look different for each person: work, volunteering, school, relationships, being a neighbour, being a customer
- Support means doing things with the person, not for them, and stepping back as their independence grows
- Connects to self-determination: the person sets the direction of their own life
- Gives a concrete example of what this would look like on a shift

questions.text: Scenario - Public Escalation: While taking a bus to an activity, the person you're supporting hits another passenger. What would you do?
questions.answerKey:
- Immediate safety first: put space between the person supported and the other passenger, check on the passenger, ask the driver to stop or get off at the next stop
- Calm, quiet voice and low demand, no lecturing or restraining as a first response; uses Mandt de-escalation and avoids a power struggle in front of an audience
- Considers what triggered it: crowding, noise, pain, unmet need, or a known pattern in the person's behaviour support plan
- Moves to a quieter setting, gives time to regulate, then decides with the person whether to continue or return home
- Notifies the manager as soon as safe, exchanges information or offers first aid to the passenger, and involves police or ambulance if there is injury
- Documents as an incident with factual detail, debriefs with the person and the team afterward, and monitors their own regulation

questions.text: If the individual's behavior escalates further, how would you handle it?
questions.answerKey:
- Keeps own regulation first: lowers voice and pace, checks body language, gives space rather than crowding or matching the escalation
- Follows the person's individual support guidelines, safety plan or behaviour support plan, and what is known to work for that person
- Reduces demands and triggers: removes the audience, limits verbal input, offers real choices, avoids power struggles over the original request
- Attends to safety of the person, other people supported and self; knows exit routes and when to step back or call for a second staff
- Physical intervention (Mandt) only as a last resort, within training, and never as a consequence or to win compliance
- Calls the on-call or manager when the situation exceeds what one staff can manage, and calls emergency services if there is serious risk of harm
- Afterwards: reconnection and repair with the person, incident documentation at the correct tier, and debrief with the manager

questions.text: Reporting Abuse: If you witnessed a co-worker abusing an individual in any way, how would you respond? (Briefly explain the reporting procedure.)
questions.answerKey:
- Intervenes immediately if the person supported is at risk, and makes sure the person is safe and cared for
- Names duty to report clearly: this is a legal obligation, it belongs to the individual staff member, and it is not optional or delayed by whether a supervisor agrees
- Reports to the manager or on-call right away, and reports externally to MCFD or the designated authority as required; police if a criminal offence
- Understands this is a reportable incident and that a protocol investigation may follow; cooperates fully and does not investigate or interview the person themselves
- Documents facts only, promptly and objectively: what was seen and heard, times, who was present, no assumptions or conclusions
- Does not warn or confront the co-worker in a way that compromises the investigation, and does not discuss the matter with other staff or people supported

questions.text: What would you do if an individual refused their medication?
questions.answerKey:
- Respects that the person has the right to refuse; does not force, hide medication in food, coax or pressure
- Explores the refusal in a low key way: pain, side effects, timing, mistrust, wanting control; offers to try again a bit later
- Knows the medication and what refusing it may mean for that person, and treats a missed critical medication as urgent
- Notifies the manager or on-call, and follows the direction in the person's support guidelines about who else is contacted (pharmacist, physician, family or guardian)
- Documents the refusal accurately on the medication record and in the daily notes, including what was offered and any follow up
- Notes the difference for PRN medication, where the person's choice not to take it is expected and simply recorded

questions.text: Supporting Medical Needs: Have you supported individuals with medical needs? If yes, please detail your experience
questions.answerKey:
- Gives concrete examples: medication administration and records, seizure support, diabetes, G tube or feeding support, mobility and transfers, personal care, appointments
- Describes following written direction from the person's plan and health professionals rather than improvising
- Shows accurate documentation and reporting of changes in health, and knows who to call and when (manager or on-call, nurse, physician, 911)
- Maintains dignity, privacy and consent during personal or medical care, and works at the person's pace
- Names relevant certification or training (first aid, medication administration, Narcan or naloxone) and is honest about gaps and willingness to be trained

questions.text: Interest and Requirements: Based on this interview, are you still interested in the position?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm a clear yes or no after hearing the full role description
- Confirm the candidate understands and accepts the practical realities discussed: shift pattern, awake or overnight hours, single staffing, locations and travel
- Note any hesitation or conditions the candidate raises so it can be followed up before an offer
- Confirm availability and earliest possible start date

questions.text: Do you have any of the following requirements? (Let the applicant know these are required prior to orientation.)
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm current criminal record check for working with children and vulnerable adults, or willingness to complete one
- Confirm valid class 5 driver's licence, driver's abstract and access to a reliable insured vehicle where the role requires it
- Confirm current first aid and CPR certification
- Confirm legal eligibility to work in Canada and required immunisation or health documentation
- Note which items are already held versus outstanding, and remind the candidate all are required prior to orientation

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?
questions.answerKey:
- Asks questions showing preparation about the people supported, the program and the team
- Asks practical questions about training, orientation, supervision and on-call support
- Asks about scheduling, shift structure and how staff are supported after a difficult incident
- Note the quality and focus of questions; no questions at all is worth following up on

name: Manager, External
description: External applicants for a Manager posting.

questions.text: Hi, . We've scheduled an hour for this interview. Sometimes it doesn't take a full hour and we want you to know that it is not an indication of how the interview went. We will start by asking you some questions, and when we are finished feel free to ask us any questions you have. How does that sound?
How did you hear about our agency?
questions.answerKey:
- States the source clearly: job posting, referral, past contact with the agency, sector network
- Names any current or former Milieu employee who referred them, for follow up
- Shows some familiarity with Milieu's services (youth, adult, community inclusion) rather than only the posting title
- Interviewer to note any prior connection to the agency or to a person supported that could be a conflict

questions.text: What skills, experience and education do you have that make you an ideal candidate for this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Direct experience supporting children, youth or adults with diversabilities, and experience supervising or scheduling staff
- Relevant education or credentials (social work, CYC, human services diploma or degree) plus current certifications such as first aid, Mandt, naloxone
- Concrete supervisory examples: coaching a team member, managing an incident, covering a vacant shift, holding a difficult conversation
- Working knowledge of funder and reporting expectations (MCFD, CLBC), incident reporting tiers, and duty to report
- Person centred framing: talks about outcomes for people supported, not only administrative competence
- Self awareness about their own gaps and how they would get support or supervision

questions.text: What do you think this role entails?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a dual role: oversight of the program's day to day operation and supervision, coaching and scheduling of staff
- Names the practice side: ISPs and individual support guidelines being followed, safety and behaviour support plans current, medication and PRN practice, documentation quality
- Understands accountability upward: incident reporting, communication with families, funders and internal management, participation in protocols
- Expects to be on call, to fill shifts, and to be present in the home or program rather than office bound
- Frames the purpose as the wellbeing and goals of the people supported, not compliance for its own sake

questions.text: In your current job, give us some examples of something you have done to be a leader?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific example with the situation, their action and the result, not a description of a job title
- Shows leading by example: taking the hard shift, modelling de-escalation, working alongside staff
- Example of coaching or developing someone: feedback given, follow up, change observed
- Example of holding a boundary or making an unpopular decision in the interest of a person supported
- Evidence of including the team in decisions and of debriefing after difficult events

questions.text: What are some specific qualities of an excellent leader you've worked for?
questions.answerKey:
- Names concrete qualities with an example: available and responsive, consistent, clear expectations
- Values a leader who gives direct feedback and follows through, not only praise
- Notes support during critical incidents and debriefing afterwards
- Mentions fairness and transparency in scheduling and decisions
- Connects leadership qualities to quality of support for people supported and to staff retention

questions.text: What did you like best about your current or last job
questions.answerKey:
- Specific aspects of the work rather than generalities, ideally relational and practice based
- Satisfaction linked to outcomes for people supported or to developing staff
- Realistic tone: enjoys the work while acknowledging its demands
- Suggests fit with a residential or community program environment

questions.text: What did you like least about your current or last job?
questions.answerKey:
- Names something honestly without disparaging former colleagues, employers or people supported
- Describes what they did about it: raised it appropriately, adapted, or set a boundary
- Distinguishes frustration with systems or workload from frustration with people
- Answer does not reveal a pattern of avoiding accountability, supervision or documentation
- Interviewer to note whether the dislike is inherent to this role (paperwork, on call, shift coverage)

questions.text: If I asked your current/previous supervisor to describe you in two words, what would he/she say?
questions.answerKey:
- Offers two specific words and backs each with an example or a piece of feedback actually received
- Words reflect qualities the role needs: reliable, calm, organised, direct, approachable
- Shows the candidate has had real supervisory conversations and can recall them accurately
- Willing to name a word that is not purely flattering

questions.text: What was the most recent suggestion your supervisor gave you for performance improvement?
questions.answerKey:
- Names an actual piece of feedback rather than deflecting or claiming none was given
- Describes their initial reaction honestly and shows they took it without defensiveness
- Explains the concrete change made and how they knew it worked
- Shows they seek feedback and use supervision rather than waiting for a review
- Interviewer to note if the answer suggests no recent supervision relationship at all

questions.text: What would you do if one of your staff was not prepared for their shift
questions.answerKey:
- Deals with immediate safety and coverage first: makes sure the person supported is safe and the shift can run
- Speaks with the staff member privately and curiously, checks what got in the way rather than assuming
- Is specific about what preparation means here: reading the log and communication book, knowing the ISP and individual support guidelines, safety and behaviour plans, medication and appointments for the day
- Sets a clear expectation, offers practical coaching or shadowing, and names a follow up point
- Documents the conversation and informs their own manager if the lapse affected a person supported or triggered an incident report
- Considers whether it is a systems issue (handover, orientation, scheduling) rather than only an individual issue

questions.text: What would you do if the coaching does not work
questions.answerKey:
- Escalates in steps: revisits expectations in writing, sets measurable goals and timelines, increases check ins
- Rules out barriers first: training gaps, health or personal circumstances, unclear direction, wrong shift fit
- Consults their own manager and human resources before formal discipline, and follows the agency's progressive process
- Keeps clear, factual, dated documentation of each conversation and each expectation set
- Acts sooner and involves the manager immediately if the conduct puts a person supported at risk, involves an allegation, or triggers duty to report
- Prepared to move to formal performance management or ending employment when the standard is not met, while treating the staff member with respect

questions.text: Tell us what type of supervision or supports you need to function in your role
questions.answerKey:
- Names concrete supports: regular one to one with their own manager, access to on call after hours, clarity on decision making authority and spending limits
- Wants direction on what to bring forward immediately (incidents, protocols, staffing risk) versus what to handle and report on later
- Uses supervision for reflective practice and debriefing after serious incidents, not only task check ins
- Describes how they support their own team the same way, including debriefs and coaching, and models asking for help
- Shows self awareness about workload, own regulation and when they need to step back or hand off
- Comfortable working independently across sites while staying in contact with peers and other program managers

questions.text: What is a Protocol Investigation?
questions.answerKey:
- Understands it as a formal investigation, MCFD or internal to the agency, usually following an allegation involving a person supported
- Triggered by suspected abuse or neglect, or a serious allegation against a staff member or caregiver
- Immediate steps: ensure the person supported is safe, report as required, notify their manager, and preserve the account without leading questions or conducting their own investigation
- Knows staff may be placed off shift or reassigned during the process, and that this is not a finding of guilt
- Documentation is factual, timely and separates observation from opinion; confidentiality is maintained throughout
- Recognises the manager's role in supporting the person supported, the team and the staff member involved while the process runs

questions.text: Have you been involved in one?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm whether they have direct experience and in what role: reporter, supervisor of the staff involved, or subject of the investigation
- What they actually did: how the report was made, who was notified, how they documented
- How they handled the team during and after, including rumour control, coverage and confidentiality
- What the outcome was and what they changed in practice afterwards
- Speaks about it without disclosing identifying details of people supported or staff

questions.text: What does the term "self-determination" mean to you?
questions.answerKey:
- The person supported directs their own life and choices; staff role is to inform options and support the decision, not to make it for them
- Gives practical examples: daily choices about routine, food, activities, who provides support, and larger choices about goals in their plan
- Recognises dignity of risk, and the difference between a choice they disagree with and a genuine safety issue that requires a plan and escalation
- Supports communication and decision making for people who use alternate communication or need supported decision making
- As a manager, holds the team to this: reviews plans and language for staff driven goals, challenges practice that is convenience or compliance based

questions.text: Tell us some experiences you have had with your family and friends growing up, and recently, that has or will help you in this job and in the field?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives real examples rather than general statements about being a caring person
- Draws a clear line to practice: patience, humour, holding boundaries, sitting with someone in distress, advocating within systems
- Shows awareness of their own background and how it shapes reactions, including what they find hard
- Understands the difference between personal experience as insight and personal experience as an unresolved trigger, and how they manage that at work
- Maintains appropriate boundaries about what they would and would not share with people supported or staff

questions.text: What does professional confidentiality mean to you? Is there a time that you would ever break confidentiality? (looking to see if they know procedure for Duty to Report)
questions.answerKey:
- Information about a person supported is shared only with those who need it to provide support, and not with family, friends or on social media
- States clearly that confidentiality is broken when there is suspected abuse, neglect or risk of harm, and that duty to report is a legal obligation on every person, not something delegated to a supervisor
- Reports directly to the ministry or authority as required and also notifies their own manager; does not wait to gather proof or investigate first
- Also names risk of harm to self or others as a limit, and follows incident reporting requirements
- Tells the person supported what they can about the limits of confidentiality where it is safe and appropriate to do so
- As a manager, ensures staff know their individual duty and cannot be discouraged from reporting

questions.text: The Youth or Adult's that arrive in our services are there for various reasons. What do you think some of the challenges and barriers are for them?
questions.answerKey:
- Names trauma, loss, disrupted attachment and multiple placements or moves, and how these show up in behaviour and trust
- Systemic barriers: housing, income, transportation, waitlists, transition from youth to adult services, loss of supports at nineteen
- Stigma and low expectations, including barriers to employment, education and being included in their community
- Substance use, mental health and unmet health needs, and the overdose risk that makes naloxone response relevant
- Barriers for Indigenous and newcomer people supported, cultural connection and family reunification
- Frames these as barriers in the person's environment and history rather than as deficits in the person

questions.text: Tell us about your experience working with people who display challenging behaviours
questions.answerKey:
- Describes specific populations and settings worked in, including single staffed and residential environments
- Relies on knowing the person: their individual support guidelines, safety or behaviour support plan, triggers and early warning signs
- Prevention focus: routine, environment, relationship and meeting needs early rather than reacting at the peak
- Trained in de-escalation and physical intervention (Mandt or equivalent) and clear that restraint is a last resort within the plan
- Follows through afterwards: debrief with the person supported and staff, incident documentation, and review of the plan if patterns are emerging
- As a manager, coaches staff who are stuck in power struggles and reviews incident data for trends

questions.text: Give an example of challenging behaviour you have witnessed?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives one specific incident with enough detail to picture it, not a general description
- Describes what happened before the incident, including setting, time of day and what preceded it
- Reports behaviour factually and without labels or sensationalising, and protects identifying details
- Includes their own read of the risk to the person supported, other people supported and staff
- Willing to include a situation that did not go well and what they learned

questions.text: In these situations, how did you respond and what you did?
questions.answerKey:
- Attended to safety first: space, exits, reducing audience, moving other people supported away
- Regulated themselves before responding: lowered voice and pace, non threatening posture, no ultimatums or countdowns
- Reduced demands and gave time and choice rather than winning the point; avoided a power struggle
- Followed the person's individual support guidelines and safety plan, using physical intervention only as a last resort within their training
- Reconnected and repaired afterwards, gave the person a chance to talk when calm, and did not carry it into the next shift
- Documented and reported at the correct incident level, notified the manager or on call, and debriefed the staff involved

questions.text: In these situations, what did you think the behaviour was telling you?
questions.answerKey:
- Reads behaviour as communication of an unmet need: pain, hunger, fatigue, sensory overload, fear, or feeling unheard
- Considers trauma and attachment history, including testing whether adults will stay and be safe
- Looks for control and choice being taken away, or a transition, change of staff or change of routine as the trigger
- Considers communication barriers and whether the person had a way to say no or ask for a break
- Reflects on the staff contribution: tone, demands, timing, too many people in the room
- Links this thinking back to changing the plan and environment rather than changing the person

questions.text: As we know sometimes in this field individuals may show physical or verbal aggression towards you. Tell us how do you not take this personally?
questions.answerKey:
- Frames the behaviour as coming from distress and history, not from a judgement about them personally
- Knows their own triggers and physical signs of activation, and has concrete strategies: stepping out, breathing, swapping with a coworker where staffing allows
- Uses debriefing and supervision rather than carrying it alone, and separates work from home
- Honest that it can still hurt or be frightening, and that acknowledging that is part of staying safe and regulated
- Does not tolerate everything: still reports incidents, addresses safety, and asks for plan review where risk is ongoing
- As a manager, normalises debriefs for staff, watches for burnout and vicarious trauma, and connects staff to supports

questions.text: How have you adapted or modified your approach when working with people from different cultures or beliefs?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete example rather than a statement of values, naming what was actually changed: food, prayer or observance times, gender of support staff, language used, family involvement in decisions
- Asks the person supported and their family what matters to them rather than assuming from background, and builds it into the support plan and daily routines
- Uses interpreters, translated material or community connections when language is a barrier, and checks understanding rather than assuming agreement
- Shows awareness of their own assumptions and describes a time they got it wrong, asked, and corrected course
- As a manager, coaches staff on the same and builds cultural practice into orientation, shift routines and team meetings

questions.text: What qualities do you think are important when representing the agency?
questions.answerKey:
- Integrity and accountability: does what they said they would do, owns mistakes rather than managing perceptions
- Professionalism in the community: aware they are visible to neighbours, funders, schools and families, and that the person supported has a reputation in that community too
- Confidentiality and discretion, including in public settings, vehicles and on social media
- Person centred and respectful language about people supported, in front of others and behind closed doors
- Reliability in relationships with MCFD, CLBC, schools and community partners: responsive, prepared, follows through on commitments
- Models the behaviour they expect from staff rather than only stating it

questions.text: How would you, as the manager support your staff team to engage with an individual to connect, participate and build relationships within their communities/ or with their neighbours?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts from the person's own interests, history and goals in their ISP rather than a generic activity list, and involves the person in choosing
- Coaches staff to support connection rather than do it for the person: introductions, natural supports, fading back so relationships belong to the person and not to staff
- Practical enabling: scheduling, transport, budget, shift planning so community time is not the first thing dropped when the home is busy
- Works with real barriers such as anxiety, behaviour, sensory needs or past negative experience by starting small, planning for hard moments, and reviewing what worked
- Builds and maintains relationships with neighbours, businesses and community groups, and deals with neighbour concerns directly and respectfully
- Follows up in supervision and team meetings, tracks progress in documentation, and celebrates small wins so staff stay motivated

questions.text: Can you please tell us about your understanding of, and experience in using, First Nations cultural interventions, backgrounds, and history?
questions.answerKey:
- Honest about the limits of their own knowledge and experience rather than overstating it
- Awareness of residential schools, the Sixties Scoop and the ongoing over representation of Indigenous children and youth in care, and how that shapes mistrust of agencies
- Names practices they have supported: connection to band, community and extended family, cultural workers or Elders, ceremony, smudging, cultural camps, land based activity
- Understands the role of the person's Nation, delegated agencies and MCFD requirements around cultural planning, and works with them rather than around them
- Follows the person's and family's lead on what culture means to them; does not treat Indigenous identity as one thing
- As a manager, builds cultural connection into the plan and supervision rather than treating it as an occasional event

questions.text: Describe ways you would support a person who does not communicate verbally
questions.answerKey:
- Learns the person's own communication: gestures, vocalisations, facial expression, body language, behaviour as communication, and what each one usually means
- Uses the tools that work for that person: picture exchange, symbols, objects of reference, signs, communication device, yes/no systems, offering real choices
- Reads the individual support guidelines and consults people who know the person well, including family and long standing staff, then verifies rather than assuming
- Gives time, one message at a time, checks back that they understood correctly, and does not talk over the person or about them as if absent
- Watches for changes in behaviour as a sign of pain, illness or distress and follows up rather than treating it as behaviour alone
- As a manager, ensures the person's communication approach is documented, taught to new staff and used consistently across the team

questions.text: Describe a time you needed to mitigate a conflict between staff
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a real situation with enough detail to judge: what the conflict was, who was involved, what the impact on people supported was
- Spoke with each staff member separately first, listened without taking sides, and separated facts from interpretation
- Brought them together with a clear focus on the effect on people supported and on the work, not on personality
- Set concrete expectations going forward and followed up, rather than assuming one conversation fixed it
- Knew when it moved beyond team conflict into a performance, harassment or reportable matter and escalated appropriately
- Documented the conversations and outcomes, and reflects on their own regulation and any bias they had to manage

questions.text: Tell me about the most difficult person you have supported. What made it difficult and what did you do
questions.answerKey:
- Frames the difficulty as the situation or the behaviour rather than labelling the person, and speaks about them respectfully
- Describes what was actually happening: aggression, refusal of support, elopement, self harm, complex medical or family dynamics, and what the behaviour was communicating
- Looked for the function and triggers, adjusted the approach, and used de-escalation that avoided power struggles rather than winning the moment
- Worked with the team, family, plans and outside professionals rather than solo, and updated guidelines or the safety plan as things were learned
- Names the effect on their own regulation and what they did about it: debriefing, support, breaks, seeking supervision
- Says what changed for the person supported over time, and what they would do differently

questions.text: What would you to if you heard a staff talking about one of the individuals we support in a negative light
questions.answerKey:
- Addresses it at the time rather than letting it pass, and does so where people supported cannot overhear
- Speaks to the staff member directly and non punitively first: what was said, how it lands, why it matters to the person's dignity and to the team culture
- Distinguishes venting or burnout from disrespect, and offers debriefing or supervision where the staff member is struggling
- Redirects to describing behaviour objectively and to the person's plan rather than judgement or labels
- Recognises when it goes further than negative talk into disrespect, neglect or abuse and triggers duty to report and the incident process
- Follows up: documents the conversation, monitors whether it continues, and escalates through progressive discipline if it does; reinforces expectations with the whole team without singling anyone out

questions.text: What would you do if your staff were not properly documenting individuals' goal progress
questions.answerKey:
- Finds out why first: unclear expectations, no time on shift, poor systems, forms that do not fit, or unwillingness
- Retrains and models it, including sitting with staff to show what a useful goal note looks like versus a task log
- Explains the purpose rather than just the requirement: goal progress drives ISP reviews, funder reporting, continuity between staff and the person's actual outcomes
- Puts practical supports in place: time in the shift routine, prompts, checking documentation regularly rather than only at review time
- Gives clear timelines and follows up, moving to supervision and progressive discipline if the pattern continues
- Documents coaching conversations and keeps their manager informed where it affects contract or licensing obligations

questions.text: What steps would you take if an individual says they have a complaint
questions.answerKey:
- Takes it seriously and listens without defensiveness, even if the complaint is about them or their team
- Makes sure the person knows their right to complain, and supports them to do it in their own way, including with an advocate, family member or communication support
- Follows the agency complaint process and tells the person what will happen next and in what timeframe
- Escalates immediately if the complaint involves abuse, neglect or harm: duty to report, incident reporting, and notification of the manager, MCFD or CLBC as required
- Documents the complaint accurately in the person's words and records the follow up
- Closes the loop: goes back to the person with the outcome and checks whether they feel it was resolved, and does not allow any retaliation

questions.text: How do you support staff to know that you care about the team but that the individual comes first?
questions.answerKey:
