- Names it openly as a shared standard rather than a threat: everyone here is accountable to the people we support, including the manager
- Shows care for staff concretely: scheduling, debriefing after hard incidents, being reachable, recognising good work, checking in on wellbeing
- Holds the line when staff convenience and the person's needs conflict, and can give an example of doing so
- Coaches rather than just corrects, and separates the person from the practice when giving feedback
- Models it themselves: knows the people supported, spends time on the floor, does not ask staff to do what they will not do
- Understands that staff who feel supported and regulated give better support, so team wellbeing and person centred practice are not in competition

questions.text: Describe a time when you were required to provide medical assistance or treatment to another person
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific incident: what happened, what they observed, what they did in what order
- Acted within their training and scope: first aid, CPR, naloxone, seizure response, epi-pen, PRN medication as directed, and called 911 where indicated
- Stayed regulated and managed the environment, including other people supported who witnessed it
- Followed up correctly: notified the manager or on-call, contacted family or guardian as appropriate, and completed incident documentation and any medication error or critical incident reporting
- States current certification honestly: first aid, CPR, medication administration, Narcan, and any gaps
- Reflects on the impact on themselves and the team, and on debriefing afterwards

questions.text: What is your experience with giving medications
questions.answerKey:
- Describes settings where they administered or oversaw medication (residential, community, youth or adult) and the level of responsibility held
- Names the practical routine: checking the medication record against the label, right person, right dose, right time, right route, signing at the time of administration rather than later
- Distinguishes scheduled medication from PRN, and can explain how a PRN decision is made, documented and followed up
- Describes safe storage, counts, receiving and disposing of medication, and narcotic or controlled medication handling
- As a manager, speaks to training and signing off staff, spot checking MAR sheets, and reviewing errors as a pattern rather than only as single events
- Mentions overdose response where relevant to the program, including Narcan

questions.text: What would you do if a staff gave an individual the wrong medication
questions.answerKey:
- First response is the health and safety of the person supported: check what was given, call the pharmacist, poison control, physician or 811, monitor and seek emergency care if indicated
- Directs the staff member to stay with the person and observe for effects, and supports that staff member so they do not panic or hide the error
- Reports up the line to their own manager or on call, and treats it under the incident reporting process, with a written incident record and the medication record corrected accurately, no back dating or altering
- Notifies family, guardian or funder contacts as required by the person's situation, and follows through on any protocol or investigation if one is opened
- Follows up with the staff member with retraining, a review of the medication process and a check for system causes such as look alike packaging or unclear directions, rather than only discipline
- Reviews whether the error is part of a wider pattern in the home and adjusts practice or supervision accordingly

questions.text: Do you have any conditions or previous injuries that would impact your ability to do the job
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can meet the physical and practical demands of the role, including driving, transfers or physical assistance where applicable, and Mandt physical intervention
- Confirm ability to work the shift pattern the role requires, including single staffed shifts, awake nights or on call if applicable
- Note any accommodation the candidate raises and flag it for follow up rather than exploring medical detail in the interview
- Record that the question was asked and answered; no scoring beyond fitness for the role and any follow up needed

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
questions.answerKey:
- Interest in staying in social services and in a leadership or supervisory role rather than treating this as a stopgap
- Realistic about growth within a multi service agency: developing staff, taking on more programs, moving between youth and adult streams
- Names concrete development goals such as further training, supervision skills, or credentials relevant to the sector
- Answer is consistent with the hours, location and commitment the role requires
- Shows commitment to the people supported and to service quality, not only to title or pay

questions.text: What questions do you have for us?
questions.answerKey:
- Asks questions that show preparation about the program, the people supported and the team they would lead
- Practical questions about staffing levels, on call expectations, single staffed sites, supervision structure and who they escalate to
- Interest in training and supports available, such as Mandt, medication sign off and orientation for new staff
- Asks about current challenges in the program or what success looks like in the first six months
- Asks about next steps and timelines; note any questions requiring follow up from the interviewer

questions.text: (If appropriate, say the following: Based on the Interview, are you still interested in this position?)
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm a clear yes or no after hearing the full scope of the role
- Confirm understanding of hours, on call, locations and travel across sites
- Note any hesitation or condition raised, such as wage, schedule or start date, for follow up
- Confirm availability and earliest start date

questions.text: Do you have training or experience with the following?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm each listed item as trained, currently certified with expiry date, or experience only, and note what needs to be completed after hire
- Expect current First Aid and CPR, Mandt or equivalent de-escalation and physical intervention, medication administration, food safe and Class 5 driver's licence with abstract as applicable to the role
- Confirm criminal record check status and willingness to complete the agency check
- For a manager, confirm experience with supervision, scheduling, incident reporting and participation in protocols or investigations
- Note relevant sector specific training such as naloxone, trauma informed practice, FASD, suicide intervention or non violent crisis response
- Ask for concrete examples where a candidate claims experience rather than formal training

name: Assistant Manager On Call, External
description: External applicants for an Assistant Manager On Call posting.

questions.text: Hi, . We've scheduled an hour for this interview. Sometimes it doesn't take a full hour and we want you to know that it is not an indication of how the interview went. We will start by asking you some questions, and when we are finished feel free to ask us any questions you have. How does that sound?
How did you hear about our agency?
questions.answerKey:
- Names the source: job board, agency website, referral from a current staff member, practicum or previous contract
- If referred, names who and whether they discussed the work realistically
- Note for follow up: any prior connection to Milieu, a program, or a person supported that may need to be checked for conflict

questions.text: What skills, experience and education do you have that make you an ideal candidate for this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Direct frontline experience with youth or adults with diversabilities, including residential and often single staffed settings
- Supervisory or lead experience: scheduling, coaching staff, giving feedback, covering shifts
- Relevant education or certification (human services, social work, child and youth care, Mandt, first aid, non violent crisis intervention, naloxone)
- Working knowledge of ISPs, individual support guidelines, safety and behaviour support plans, incident reporting and duty to report
- Concrete examples rather than general claims, including decisions made without a manager present

questions.text: What do you think this role entails?
questions.answerKey:
- Being the after hours point of contact for staff across programs: fielding calls, giving direction, problem solving in the moment
- Filling shift vacancies and arranging coverage so homes are never left unstaffed
- Supporting staff through incidents: de-escalation guidance, medical or PRN questions, elopement, police or ambulance involvement
- Knowing what must be escalated the same night to a manager or on call director, and what can wait for business hours
- Documentation and handover: incident reports, on call log, communicating to the program manager
- Coaching and supporting staff rather than only directing them, and holding boundaries around scope

questions.text: In your current job, give us some examples of something you have done to be a leader?
questions.answerKey:
- A specific example, not a description of leadership in general
- Stepping in during a difficult shift or incident and steadying the team
- Coaching or orienting a new staff member, modelling how to support a person supported
- Advocating for a person supported or bringing a concern forward through the right channel
- Taking responsibility when something went wrong, including their own part in it

questions.text: What are some specific qualities of an excellent leader you've worked for?
questions.answerKey:
- Available and responsive, especially when a staff member is alone on shift and needs direction
- Gives clear, direct feedback and follows through on what they said they would do
- Stays regulated in a crisis and debriefs afterward rather than blaming
- Fair and consistent with all staff; transparent about decisions
- Keeps the focus on the people supported and models person centred practice

questions.text: What did you like best about your current or last job
questions.answerKey:
- Names something specific and credible, ideally tied to relationships with people supported and seeing progress over time
- Values team culture, learning, or variety and problem solving in the work
- Answer aligns with what this role actually offers, including after hours responsibility
- Shows genuine interest in the population rather than a generic response

questions.text: What did you like least about your current or last job?
questions.answerKey:
- Answers honestly without disparaging former employers, coworkers or people supported
- Frames the dislike around process or systems (short staffing, unclear direction, paperwork volume) rather than personal grievance
- Describes what they did about it or how they managed their own frustration
- Note for follow up: whether the same conditions exist in this role, particularly on call demands and administrative work

questions.text: If I asked your current/previous supervisor to describe you in two words, what would he/she say?
questions.answerKey:
- Two words that fit an on call role: dependable, calm, thorough, approachable
- Backs each word with a short example or situation the supervisor would be referring to
- Self awareness rather than only flattering description
- Note for follow up: whether this supervisor is a listed reference

questions.text: What was the most recent suggestion your supervisor gave you for performance improvement?
questions.answerKey:
- Names a real piece of feedback rather than deflecting or claiming there was none
- Describes it without defensiveness and shows they understood why it was given
- States what they changed in practice and whether it held
- Openness to supervision and coaching, which matters when direction comes by phone at night

questions.text: What steps would you take if you received a call that a staff had not shown up for their shift?
questions.answerKey:
- First priority is confirming whether the person or people supported are currently safe and whether a staff member is alone or past the end of their shift
- Attempts to contact the absent staff member directly to confirm safety and whether they are en route
- Works the call out process to fill the shift: available casuals, staff qualified for that program, overtime as needed, keeping the outgoing staff on shift until relief arrives
- Considers program specific needs when matching coverage: medication administration, individual support guidelines, behaviour support or safety plans, training required for that home
- Attends in person or arranges another qualified person if no coverage can be found, so the home is not left unstaffed
- Notifies the program manager or on call director per escalation expectations, and communicates clearly with the staff already on shift
- Follows up afterward: no shift is handled as a performance matter by the manager, not addressed punitively at 2am

questions.text: What kind of documentation would you need to complete?
questions.answerKey:
- On call log entry: time of the call, who called, what was reported, what direction was given and by whom
- Record of coverage attempts: who was contacted, outcome, who was assigned, actual hours worked for payroll and scheduling
- Incident report at the correct tier (general, critical or reportable) if anything happened during the gap in coverage
- Written handover to the program manager for business hours follow up, including any staffing or performance concern
- Documentation is factual, objective and timely, written the same shift, without opinion or speculation
- Awareness that records may be reviewed in a protocol or by a funder, and that duty to report obligations are acted on separately and immediately, not just recorded

questions.text: Tell us what type of supervision or supports you need to function in your role
questions.answerKey:
- Names concrete supports: clear expectations, access to a manager or on call peer, debriefs after difficult shifts, and written direction such as individual support guidelines and safety plans
- Comfortable working independently and making decisions in the moment, which the on call role requires, while knowing which decisions go up the line first
- Asks for direction early rather than after a situation escalates, and checks in when unsure of a person's plan
- Uses supervision for reflection and feedback, not only for task sign off, and can name how they take feedback
- Awareness of their own regulation and workload limits, including using debriefing and time off after critical incidents

questions.text: What is a Protocol Investigation?
questions.answerKey:
- An MCFD or internal agency investigation, usually following an allegation involving a person supported
- Understands it can involve staff conduct, alleged abuse or neglect, or a serious incident, and that it is a formal process with external oversight
- Role of the manager or on call is to make sure the person supported is safe, preserve information, write accurate factual documentation and cooperate fully
- Does not investigate independently, does not question the person supported or coach staff on what to say, does not discuss the matter outside those who need to know
- Recognises staff may be reassigned or on leave during the process and that confidentiality is maintained throughout

questions.text: Have you been involved in one?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms whether they have participated, and in what capacity: reporter, witness, supervisor supporting staff, or subject of the process
- Describes their part without naming identifying details of people supported or staff
- Can explain what they contributed: timely reporting, factual documentation, cooperating with the investigator
- Shows what they learned about supporting a team and a person supported through an unsettling process
- If no direct experience, describes how they would approach it and where they would seek direction

questions.text: What does the term "self-determination" mean to you?
questions.answerKey:
- People supported making their own choices about their daily life, goals, relationships and risks, including choices staff would not make
- Supporting informed choice: presenting options in a way the person understands rather than steering toward the easiest outcome
- Balancing dignity of risk with duty of care, and knowing when a risk needs a manager, a safety plan or a team discussion
- Practical examples: what to eat, how to spend money, who to see, what goals go in their ISP, when to say no to an activity
- Recognises where staff power and routine can quietly override a person's choice and how to check for that in a team

questions.text: Tell us some experiences you have had with your family and friends growing up, and recently, that has or will help you in this job and in the field?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives real examples rather than general statements about liking people
- Shows understanding of family systems, caregiving, or supporting someone through hardship, and what it taught them
- Reflects on difference and inclusion in their own life and how that shapes non judgemental practice
- Demonstrates self awareness about what they bring from their own history and where their triggers or blind spots sit
- Shows current supports and boundaries in their own life that keep them steady in demanding work

questions.text: What does professional confidentiality mean to you? Is there a time that you would ever break confidentiality? (looking to see if they know procedure for Duty to Report)
questions.answerKey:
- Information about people supported is shared only with those who need it to provide support, not with family, friends or other staff outside the team
- Names duty to report: suspected abuse, neglect or a child in need of protection is reported to MCFD, and this obligation is personal and cannot be delegated away
- Also breaks confidentiality where there is risk of harm to self or others, or a medical emergency
- Tells the person supported, where appropriate, what will be shared and with whom
- Follows up with the manager and completes incident documentation, and understands general, critical and reportable incident tiers
- Practical awareness of confidentiality in daily life: social media, community settings, phone calls, records left in view

questions.text: The Youth or Adult's that arrive in our services are there for various reasons. What do you think some of the challenges and barriers are for them?
questions.answerKey:
- Trauma, loss, disrupted attachment and multiple placements or moves
- Systemic barriers: poverty, housing, transport, waitlists, stigma, racism, and for Indigenous people the impact of colonisation and child welfare history
- Practical barriers to independence: limited income, employment access, transition to adulthood and loss of supports at age milestones
- Health and mental health, substance use and overdose risk, and limited access to appropriate services
- Isolation and lack of natural supports, few people in their life who are not paid to be there
- Frames these as barriers in the person's environment rather than deficits in the person

questions.text: Tell us about your experience working with people who display challenging behaviours
questions.answerKey:
- Concrete settings and populations, with the type of behaviour described respectfully and without labelling the person
- Familiarity with behaviour support plans, safety plans and individual support guidelines, and following them consistently
- Training and frameworks: Mandt or similar de-escalation, trauma informed practice, physical intervention only as a last resort within training
- Emphasis on prevention and pattern spotting: known triggers, routines, environment, relationship as the primary tool
- Documentation and debriefing after incidents, and using that information to adjust supports
- As a supervisor, coaching staff through incidents and supporting consistency across a team

questions.text: Give an example of challenging behaviour you have witnessed?
questions.answerKey:
- A specific incident with enough context to judge: setting, what led up to it, what happened
- Describes the behaviour factually without sensationalising or using clinical labels
- Includes what was happening for the person beforehand, not just the peak moment
- Notes safety considerations for the person, other people supported and staff
- Maintains confidentiality while telling the example

questions.text: In these situations, how did you respond and what you did?
questions.answerKey:
- Regulated themselves first: tone, pace, body language, distance
- Reduced demands and stimulation, gave space and time, avoided a power struggle over compliance or winning
- Attended to safety of everyone present, including removing others or themselves if needed
- Followed the person's known plan and used physical intervention only as a last resort within training
- Reconnected and repaired with the person afterwards, once they were settled
- Documented the incident, reported at the right tier, notified the manager or on call, and debriefed with staff

questions.text: In these situations, what did you think the behaviour was telling you?
questions.answerKey:
- Reads behaviour as communication of an unmet need rather than manipulation or defiance
- Names plausible drivers: fear, pain or illness, sensory overload, hunger or fatigue, loss of control, anniversary or contact with family, communication difficulty
- Links to trauma and attachment where relevant, including testing whether adults will stay
- Looks for patterns across time, staff and settings rather than a single explanation
- Turns the interpretation into a change in support: adjusting environment, routine, staffing or the plan, in consultation with the team

questions.text: What steps would you take if you received an emergency call from a staff due to an incident occurring with a person supported
questions.answerKey:
- Stays calm, gets a clear picture: is anyone injured, where is the person supported now, who else is present, is the staff member safe
- Directs immediate safety steps first, including calling 911, first aid, naloxone or police as the situation requires
- Attends in person when the situation needs it, or arranges additional staffing or relief support
- Gives clear direction grounded in the person's safety plan or individual support guidelines rather than improvising
- Notifies the manager on call and follows the incident reporting tier: general, critical or reportable, including MCFD or CLBC notification and duty to report where applicable
- Follows up after: documentation completed and reviewed, debrief with the staff member, checks in on the person supported and any others affected, and reviews whether the plan needs changing

questions.text: How have you adapted or modified your approach when working with people from different cultures or beliefs?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete example of asking a person supported or their family what matters to them rather than assuming from background
- Adjusted practical supports: food, prayer or observance, gender of support worker, holidays, language or interpreter use
- Recognises culture, faith and identity belong in the ISP and individual support guidelines, and follows what is documented there
- Shows willingness to say they did not know something and to learn, rather than claiming expertise in every culture
- Holds the line where a belief or practice conflicts with safety or rights, and takes that to a manager rather than deciding alone

questions.text: What qualities do you think are important when representing the agency?
questions.answerKey:
- Integrity and accountability: does what they said they would do, owns errors, does not hide problems from managers
- Professional boundaries and confidentiality, including in the community, with families, landlords, police, hospital staff and the public
- Calm and respectful under pressure, particularly on call when reaching staff who are stressed or a situation is escalating
- Speaks about people supported respectfully at all times, including when they are not present
- Understands they represent Milieu to funders and partners such as MCFD, CLBC and VSB, and to neighbours and community members

questions.text: Tell me about the most difficult person you have supported. What made it difficult and what did you do
questions.answerKey:
- Describes the behaviour or situation, not the person, as the difficulty, and avoids blaming or labelling
- Looks for the function or driver behind the behaviour: trauma, pain, communication, unmet need, environment, change in routine
- Concrete actions taken: adjusting approach, following the behaviour support or safety plan, giving space, avoiding a power struggle, consistency across shifts
- Names their own reaction honestly and what they did to stay regulated, and when they stepped back or handed over to a colleague
- Brought it to the team or manager and to documentation rather than managing it privately, and reviewed what worked over time
- Reflects on what they would do differently and shows the relationship improved or was maintained

questions.text: In addition to responding to emergency calls there will be required documentation and reporting. How will you ensure timely and accurate reporting?
questions.answerKey:
- Documents at the time or immediately after the call rather than at the end of the on call shift, while detail is accurate
- Distinguishes general, critical and reportable incidents and knows each carries its own process and timeline
- Writes objectively: what was reported, times, who was involved, what direction was given, what follow up is outstanding
- Practical system for tracking multiple calls across a shift: a log or notes, and a clear handover to the incoming on call and the program manager
- Follows up to confirm staff completed their own incident reports and that any external reporting obligation, including duty to report, was met
- Recognises documentation is a record for the person supported, for funders and for any protocol that may follow

questions.text: What would you do if the staff called to report a medication error?
questions.answerKey:
- First question is the wellbeing of the person supported: what was given, how much, when, and how the person is presenting now
- Directs staff to contact Poison Control, pharmacist, physician or 911 as the situation requires, and to stay with and monitor the person
- Stays calm with the staff member so they report fully and do not minimise, and reinforces that reporting an error is the right thing to do
- Ensures the error and follow up are documented, an incident report is completed, and the medication record reflects what actually happened
- Notifies the program manager and follows the incident reporting process, including notification to family or guardian and funder where required
- Follow up afterwards on cause and prevention, retraining or system change, rather than treating it only as an individual fault

questions.text: Do you have any conditions or previous injuries that would impact your ability to do the job
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can perform the physical demands: driving, responding on site at short notice, Mandt physical intervention, personal care and transfers where required
- Note any accommodation the candidate raises and refer to the manager or HR for follow up, without asking for diagnostic detail
- Confirm they are aware the role involves after hours calls and overnight availability
- Record the answer only; no rating of quality beyond a yes or no and any follow up needed

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
questions.answerKey:
- Goals that fit a community social services career and are realistic against what Milieu can offer
- Interest in growing into leadership, supervision, training or a specific program stream rather than a vague answer
- Some indication of intended stability, given on call work depends on staff knowing and trusting the person in the role
- Interest in continued training and development, for example Mandt, medication, trauma informed practice
- Honest about other commitments such as study or a second role, and how those fit with on call availability

questions.text: What questions do you have for us?
questions.answerKey:
- Asks questions showing they have thought about the role: on call rotation, call volume, geographic coverage, back up from managers
- Asks about the people supported and the programs, not only about pay and schedule
- Asks about supervision, orientation, training and how decisions are escalated after hours
- Interviewer notes any questions requiring follow up on pay, hours, mileage or start date

questions.text: (If appropriate, say the following: Based on the Interview, are you still interested in this position?)
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes or no after hearing what the role involves
- Any hesitation named, for example on call hours, travel across sites or overnight calls
- Confirm availability for the on call rotation and expected start date
- Record the response for follow up; no scoring beyond this

questions.text: Do you have training or experience with the following?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm current certificates and expiry dates: first aid, Mandt, medication administration, Narcan or naloxone, food safe, class 5 licence and driving abstract
- Confirm criminal record check and any prior clearance, plus WHMIS or other required training
- Note relevant experience by stream: youth residential, adult residential, shared living, community inclusion, employment services, outreach
- Note experience with incident reporting, supervising or scheduling staff, and being on call
- Flag any gaps as training Milieu would need to provide before or shortly after start

questions.text: What interests you about the position you have applied for?
questions.answerKey:
- Specific interest in this program stream (youth residential, adult residential, community inclusion, employment) rather than a generic interest in helping people
- Wants a role that combines direct support with leading and developing a staff team, and can say why they are ready for that step now
- Connects their motivation to person centred practice and self determination for people supported
- Has looked into Milieu's services and funders and can name something concrete that drew them
- Realistic about the demands: on call, single staffed sites, shift coverage, administrative load

questions.text: What skills, experience and education do you have that make you an ideal candidate for this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Relevant direct support experience with the population, described with examples rather than a list of job titles
- Education or training in social services, child and youth care, community support work, or equivalent lived and work experience; current certifications such as Mandt, first aid, non violent crisis intervention, naloxone
- Supervisory or lead experience: scheduling, orientation of new staff, coaching, running shift handovers or team meetings
- Documentation and reporting competence: incident reports, ISP goal tracking, medication records
- Self awareness about their own regulation, boundaries, and where they still need development or supervision

questions.text: What do you think this role entails?
questions.answerKey:
- Balancing hands on shifts with oversight of the home or program day to day
- Ensuring supports are delivered as set out in each person's ISP, individual support guidelines and safety or behaviour support plans
- Supervising and coaching staff, orientation, scheduling and coverage, running team meetings and debriefs
- Incident response and reporting through the general, critical and reportable tiers, and knowing when to escalate to a manager or report externally under duty to report
- Administrative work: documentation, medication records including PRN, finances, maintenance, communication with families, funders and community partners
- Advocacy and community connection for people supported, not just compliance with paperwork

questions.text: In your current job, give us some examples of something you have done to be a leader?
questions.answerKey:
- A concrete example with their own action described, not what the team did generally
- Modelling the practice they expect: taking the harder shift, stepping in during an escalation, following through on a person's goal
- Coaching or giving feedback to a coworker directly and respectfully rather than avoiding it or escalating first
- Advocating for a person supported or for the team upward to management
- Reflection on how it landed, including what they would do differently

questions.text: How would you deal with conflicts amongst the staffing team and what steps would you take to resolve the situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Addresses it early and directly rather than letting it build or move through gossip
- Speaks with each person separately first to understand the issue, listens without taking sides
- Brings the parties together where appropriate, keeps the focus on behaviour and impact on people supported rather than personalities
- Refers back to expectations, values and respect, and agrees on specific follow up actions with a check in date
- Documents the conversation and escalates to their manager or HR when the issue involves harassment, misconduct, or risk to a person supported
- Reflects on their own reaction and stays neutral, including when they are personally part of the conflict

questions.text: What experience do you have with administrative tasks?
questions.answerKey:
- Scheduling, shift coverage, timesheets and payroll approval
- Documentation: daily notes, incident reports, ISP goal tracking, medication and PRN records, audits of files
- Program finances such as petty cash, receipts, grocery and household budgets, and money handling for people supported
- Comfort with email, databases and reporting systems, and meeting deadlines for submissions to management or funders
- Understands that records about people supported are confidential and stored and shared accordingly

questions.text: Tell us about your experience working with people who display challenging behaviours
questions.answerKey:
- Specific examples with context: setting, who they were supporting, what the behaviour looked like
- Range of situations described without sensationalising: aggression, property damage, self harm, elopement, substance use, withdrawal or refusal
- Familiarity with working from safety plans, behaviour support plans and individual support guidelines
- Training used in practice such as Mandt or other de-escalation training, and awareness that physical intervention is a last resort
- Sustained relationship with the person over time, not just crisis moments

questions.text: In these situations, how did you respond and what you did?
questions.answerKey:
- Regulated themselves first: tone, volume, body language, giving space and time
- Reduced demands and stimulation, offered choices, avoided a power struggle over compliance
- Followed the person's known plan and preferred strategies rather than improvising
- Ensured safety of the person, others present and themselves; called for support when needed
- Reconnected and repaired with the person afterwards once they were calm
- Documented, reported at the correct incident tier, and debriefed with staff and manager

questions.text: In these situations, what did you think the behavior was telling you?
questions.answerKey:
- Treats the behaviour as communication of an unmet need rather than as manipulation or defiance
- Names plausible drivers: pain or illness, sensory overload, hunger or fatigue, communication barriers, loss of control or choice
- Trauma informed framing: trigger, reminder of past experience, attachment and trust, fear of abandonment
- Considers environmental and staff factors, including how the approach or the demand may have contributed
- Looks for patterns over time using documentation rather than judging a single incident

questions.text: How would you support staff in these situations?
questions.answerKey:
- Is available and responsive during the incident, attends in person or by phone when a staff member is alone on shift
- Debriefs afterward focusing on wellbeing first, then on practice, without blame
- Coaches on the person's plan and strategies, models the approach on shift, provides refresher training such as Mandt
- Watches for staff burnout, vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue; adjusts shifts, offers EFAP or manager support
- Ensures reports are completed accurately and escalates to the manager for critical or reportable incidents and any protocol
- Brings recurring patterns back to the team and to the manager so the ISP or safety plan can be reviewed

questions.text: How would you support the staff team to engage with an individual to connect, participate and build relationships within their communities/ or with their neighbours
questions.answerKey:
- Starts from what the person supported wants and is interested in, not what is convenient for staff or already scheduled
- Builds community goals into the ISP and into shift planning so they actually happen
- Coaches staff to step back and facilitate natural relationships rather than being the person's only social contact
- Uses local resources: neighbours, recreation centres, faith and cultural groups, volunteering, employment and vocational supports
- Models it themselves on shift and recognises staff when they follow through
- Anticipates barriers such as transport, funding, anxiety or past negative experiences and problem solves them with the team
- Attends to dignity and image: age appropriate activities, presence in the community as a valued citizen

questions.text: What would you do if you observed staff were not following the schedule of the person supported?
questions.answerKey:
- Checks first whether there was a reason: the person declined, was unwell, or the schedule no longer suits them
- Talks to the staff member directly and privately, asks rather than accuses, clarifies the expectation and why the routine matters to the person supported
- Reinforces that the schedule reflects the person's choices and ISP, and that consistency supports predictability and trust
- Coaches or models the shift, follows up to see whether it changed
- Documents the conversation and escalates to the manager if the pattern continues or if the person supported is being neglected
- Raises the schedule for review with the team and the person supported if it is repeatedly unworkable

questions.text: What would you do if you observed staff supporting the person in a way that is contrary to their support plan?
questions.answerKey:
- Checks first whether the person supported is safe in the moment and steps in directly only if there is immediate risk or harm
- Speaks to the staff member privately rather than correcting them in front of the person supported or other staff
- Asks questions before assuming, since the staff member may not know the plan, may have been given informal direction, or the plan may be out of date
- Re-teaches the actual direction in the support plan or individual support guidelines and models what it looks like in practice
- Documents the conversation and follows up to confirm the practice has changed, escalating to the manager if it repeats or if the deviation caused harm
- Recognises when the situation crosses into abuse or neglect and knows duty to report and incident reporting apply regardless of the coaching conversation

questions.text: What would you do if staff did not complete appropriate documentation?
questions.answerKey:
- Names why documentation matters in practice: the next shift, medication and PRN records, incident follow up, funder and family accountability
- Addresses it early and directly with the staff member rather than quietly fixing the paperwork themselves
- Looks for the cause, whether it is workload on a single staffed shift, unclear expectations, literacy or language barriers, or a training gap
- Offers concrete support such as reviewing an example, showing the required detail, or adjusting when in the shift notes are written
- Sets a clear expectation and timeline, monitors it, and moves to the manager and formal performance process if gaps continue
- Treats missing critical or reportable incident documentation as urgent and escalates it immediately

questions.text: What are two words that a current or past supervisor would us to describe you?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives two specific words rather than a list of general positives
- Backs each word with a short concrete example from their own work
- Words that fit the role, for example dependable, calm under pressure, approachable, organised, follows through
- Shows self awareness, including some sense of how they are actually experienced by a supervisor and team

questions.text: What would you like to be doing in 5 years?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a direction that is realistic and connected to social services or leadership rather than a rehearsed answer
- Shows interest in staying with the sector and with people supported, not using the role as a short stopover
- Mentions concrete development steps such as further training, supervision skills, or growth into a program or management role
- Fits reasonably with what Milieu can offer in youth, adult or Sereno services

name: Family Services Counsellor
description: Family Services Program, Youth and Family Therapist.

questions.text: Access to vehicle?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm reliable access to a vehicle for work use, and whether it is their own or shared
- Confirm business use insurance and willingness to provide a copy
- Note any days or times the vehicle is not available, since the role involves travel across community sites and family homes
- Follow up on willingness to transport people supported if the role requires it

questions.text: Class 5 license?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm a valid BC Class 5 (or equivalent) driver's licence, not learner or restricted
- Confirm willingness to provide a current driver's abstract
- Note any restrictions or pending issues the candidate raises
- Follow up on out of province licence and timeline to transfer

questions.text: What work experiences have you had that you feel would be relevant to this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Direct counselling or family work with children, youth and caregivers, with a sense of caseload size and typical presenting issues
- Experience in the contexts this role touches: family reunification and mediation, youth in care, foster caregivers, trauma and attachment, substance use, FASD
- Familiarity with MCFD or comparable statutory involvement, including working alongside social workers and writing to funder expectations
- Relevant education, clinical supervision and specific modalities they have actually practised, not just studied
- Concrete example of a family they worked with and what changed, described respectfully and without identifying detail
- Comfort working in homes and community rather than only an office, and managing safety and boundaries in those settings

questions.text: How do you build a rapport with your team/staff members?
questions.answerKey:
- Shows up consistently and follows through on what they said they would do, treating reliability as the base of trust
- Learns the team's existing practice and the individual support guidelines before proposing changes
- Uses regular contact: check ins, shift overlap, debriefs after difficult incidents rather than only formal meetings
- Gives feedback directly and in private, and invites it about their own practice
- Recognises the expertise of residential and frontline staff who know the person supported day to day, and shares information both ways
- Names boundaries: warm and approachable while staying clear on role, confidentiality and accountability

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in 5 years from now?
questions.answerKey:
- A realistic direction that keeps them in direct practice with children, youth and families rather than a vague or unrelated plan
- Specific development goals: clinical hours, registration or designation, added training in trauma, attachment or family therapy
- Interest in growing within the agency, taking on program or supervisory responsibility, or deepening specialised work
- Signs of commitment and stability, given families need continuity of counsellor
- Honesty about any planned schooling, relocation or leave that would affect availability

questions.text: What personal and professional strengths would you bring to this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Names strengths with an example attached, not a list of adjectives
- Clinical strengths relevant here: engaging resistant or guarded youth and caregivers, trauma informed and attachment aware practice, de-escalation without power struggles
- Practical strengths: organised documentation, meeting reporting timelines, managing a caseload and competing demands
- Self regulation under pressure and ability to hold a calm presence when a family session becomes heated
- Cultural humility and adapting approach to the family's values, language and circumstances
- Collaborative habits: keeps social workers, caregivers and team informed, asks for consultation early

questions.text: Areas you're still needing to work on?
questions.answerKey:
- Names a real growth area rather than a disguised strength or a claim of having none
- Shows awareness of how it shows up in practice, for example taking on too much, difficulty saying no, discomfort with conflict, or a modality they are still building
- Describes what they are actively doing about it: supervision, training, consultation, adjusting workload
- Identifies the supports or feedback they would want from a manager here
- Openness to feedback and evidence they have acted on it before

questions.text: Describe a time when you disagreed with a supervisor on an approach
questions.answerKey:
- A real, specific instance with what the disagreement was actually about
- Raised it directly and privately with the supervisor, with reasoning grounded in the person supported or family rather than personal preference
- Distinguishes clinical difference of opinion from a safety or reporting concern, and escalates further only when the latter
- Followed the decision once made, or explains clearly why they could not and what they did instead
- Reflects on the outcome and what they would do differently, without blaming the supervisor
- Kept it out of the team and out of the family's view

questions.text: What are your thoughts on balancing confidentiality and the need to report?
questions.answerKey:
- Explains limits of confidentiality to the youth or family at the start of service and revisits them as needed
- Clear on duty to report: suspected abuse or neglect of a child or youth goes to MCFD, is not optional, and is not delayed for permission
- Also names risk of harm to self or others and court orders as limits
- Tells the person what they are reporting and why where it is safe to do so, so the relationship is not broken by surprise
- Shares on a need to know basis with the team, funder and collaterals rather than disclosing everything to everyone
- Consults a manager when unsure, and documents the concern, the decision and the report promptly and factually

questions.text: Tell us about experience in working collaboratively with professionals
questions.answerKey:
- Specific examples with named roles: MCFD social workers, schools, physicians or psychiatry, probation, foster caregivers, residential staff, cultural or Indigenous supports
- Describes their part in integrated case meetings, plan of care meetings or family conferences, including preparing and contributing written input
- Keeps the family's voice and goals central rather than letting professionals plan around them
- Handles disagreement between agencies by staying focused on the child or youth, clarifying roles, and escalating to a manager when unresolved
- Timely, accurate information sharing within consent and need to know limits
- Follows through on agreed actions and closes the loop with the other professionals

questions.text: Describe three cases from previous experience that demonstrate your ability to use very different approaches (i.e. theoretical model, length of service, client characteristics, service delivery approach)
questions.answerKey:
- Offers three genuinely different pieces of work, not three versions of the same approach
- Variation is visible in at least a few of: theoretical model used, brief versus long term service, individual versus family or dyadic work, office versus home or community delivery, voluntary versus statutory involvement
- Explains why each approach was chosen for that family: age, developmental stage, trauma history, culture, readiness, safety, mandate
- Describes adjusting or abandoning an approach when it was not working, and what they changed to
- Names outcomes honestly, including work that did not go well and what they learned
- Presents the people involved respectfully, without identifying detail or clinical labels beyond what was assessed

questions.text: What in your view are the characteristics of a good therapist?
questions.answerKey:
- Genuine warmth, curiosity and non judgement, with belief that families have capacity and the right to direct their own goals
- Clear boundaries and consistency, holding the relationship steady without rescuing or over-identifying
- Self awareness: knows their own triggers, uses supervision, manages vicarious trauma and their own regulation in session
- Flexibility to match approach to the person rather than fitting the person to a preferred model
- Cultural humility and willingness to be corrected by the family
- Practical accountability: reliable, documents well, meets reporting obligations, and works as part of a team around the family

questions.text: How have you adapted or modified your approach in working with clients from different cultures?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete example of changing how they worked, not a general statement about valuing diversity: pacing, who was invited into meetings, where the meeting happened, use of interpreters rather than family members
- Asks the family what matters to them rather than assuming from ethnicity, including how they understand parenting, discipline, mental health and help seeking
- Recognises the role of extended family, elders or community and faith leaders in decision making, and works with them rather than around them
- Names their own cultural lens and assumptions, and describes checking these with the family, a colleague or a supervisor
- Shows awareness of history and mistrust of child welfare systems, particularly for Indigenous and newcomer families, and how they build safety and transparency about MCFD involvement
- Adapts written and verbal material to language and literacy level, and confirms the family actually understood what was agreed

questions.text: What experience have you had in designing and implementing groups support groups?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes specific groups run or co-facilitated: population, size, number of sessions, setting, and their actual role
- Explains how the group content came from an identified need, and how goals for participants were set and reviewed
- Covers practical set up: screening and intake for fit, group agreements, confidentiality and its limits, attendance, transport, childcare, timing
- Describes managing group dynamics, one member dominating, disclosures in group, a participant becoming distressed, and when to follow up individually
- Mentions co-facilitation, debriefing after sessions, and documentation of attendance and progress
- Reflects on what did not work and what they changed for the next cycle

questions.text: What experience have you had with assessment tools?
questions.answerKey:
- Names specific tools they have actually used and in what context, with an honest account of their level of training and whether they were qualified to administer or only to gather information
- Describes intake and psychosocial assessment, risk and safety screening, and gathering collateral from family, school and other professionals
- Treats assessment as ongoing and relational, feeding into the support plan and goals rather than being a one time form
- Explains results to the family in plain language and uses them collaboratively rather than as a label
- Knows the limits of their scope and refers on for clinical or diagnostic assessment when indicated
- Documents accurately and distinguishes observation from interpretation

questions.text: How do you think personal issues interplay with a clinician's skills when working in this field?
questions.answerKey:
- Acknowledges directly that personal history, stress and current life events affect judgement, patience, boundaries and capacity to sit with distress
- Recognises where their own experience creates blind spots or over identification with a parent or a young person, and how they notice this in themselves
- Names concrete signs of their own dysregulation or fatigue: irritability, avoiding certain files, taking work home, dreading a visit
- Describes what they do about it: supervision, consultation with a colleague, debriefing after a difficult session, therapy, time off, adjusting caseload
- Knows when a personal issue means declining or transferring a file, or disclosing a conflict of interest to a manager
- Distinguishes appropriate self disclosure that serves the family from disclosure that meets the counsellor's own needs

name: Operational Generalist
description: Operational Generalist, a senior cross-functional leadership posting.

questions.text: Do you have a study or work permit?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms citizenship, permanent residency, or a valid study or work permit
- If a permit, note the type, expiry date and any restrictions on hours or employer
- Note any follow up needed to sight and copy the document before hire

questions.text: Do you have a valid BC driver's license? 5 7NEmployment Requirements
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms a valid BC driver's licence and class, and whether it is full or graduated
- Note access to a reliable vehicle and business use insurance if driving is part of the role
- Note willingness to provide a driver's abstract and any restrictions or pending items
- Confirms willingness to complete a criminal record check and provide references

questions.text: What do you know about Milieu? And what drew you to apply for this position?
questions.answerKey:
- Knows Milieu is a Surrey based multi-service agency supporting adults with diversabilities since 1989 and children, youth and families since 1999
- Names services accurately: residential homes, community inclusion, employment services, youth centre and learning centre, outreach, respite
- Understands funding and partnership context: MCFD, CLBC, and the school partnership with VSB
- Connects to the mission of people as valued, contributing citizens, and to values such as person-centred practice and self-determination
- Gives a genuine, specific reason for applying that links their own experience to this agency rather than a general interest in social services

questions.text: What is your general understanding of the position and your key responsibilities?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes an operations oversight role spanning multiple service areas rather than direct support of people supported
- Names concrete responsibilities: systems and process improvement, supporting directors and managers, resource and budget oversight, reporting to the executive
- Understands the work sits inside a regulated, funded environment with accreditation, contract and incident reporting obligations
- Recognises decisions ultimately affect quality of support and safety for people supported, not just efficiency
- Is clear about their own scope and when a matter goes to the CEO, a director, or an external body

questions.text: This role may require flexibility in scheduling to meet the needs of the agency. Can you share your approach to working outside of standard hours when necessary?
questions.answerKey:
- States actual availability plainly, including evenings, weekends and on call or after hours contact
- Gives examples of responding to urgent situations outside hours, such as a critical incident, staffing gap or protocol
- Distinguishes what truly needs an immediate response from what can wait for business hours
- Shows sustainable practice: planning coverage, delegating, and protecting their own recovery time so availability is not driven by crisis
- Names any known constraints honestly rather than overpromising

questions.text: Can you describe your experience working in fast-paced environments?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a specific example of a high volume or unpredictable environment and the scale involved
- Describes a practical method for triage when several things compete, with safety of people supported and staff first
- Shows they stay regulated under pressure and notice their own stress signals
- Keeps documentation and follow through intact rather than letting it slip when busy
- Uses the team: hands work off, communicates changes, and does not absorb everything alone

questions.text: What do you see as the biggest challenges in overseeing multiple departments, and how do you prioritize competing demands?
questions.answerKey:
- Names real challenges: competing funder requirements, staffing and recruitment pressure, uneven information flow between programs, and depth of knowledge across very different service streams
- Prioritises by risk first: anything affecting safety, a reportable incident or a duty to report obligation goes ahead of administrative work
- Relies on directors and managers as subject matter experts rather than trying to hold every detail personally
- Describes a working rhythm that keeps oversight current, such as regular check ins, shared trackers and clear escalation thresholds
- Is explicit about saying no or deferring lower priority work, and communicating that decision back

questions.text: Describe a time when you worked closely with a CEO or executive team to implement a major organizational strategy. What was your role, and what were the outcomes?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a specific strategy or organisational change and their own role in it, not the team's role generally
- Shows the translation work: turning executive direction into steps frontline managers and staff could actually carry out
- Gives evidence of bringing information back up to the executive, including bad news or resistance
- Names measurable or observable outcomes and what did not go well
- Demonstrates appropriate discretion with confidential executive or board level material

questions.text: Tell us about a time you identified inefficiencies across different business functions. What steps did you take to improve processes, and what was the result?
questions.answerKey:
- Identifies a concrete inefficiency and how it surfaced, such as duplicate reporting, delays, or a recurring complaint
- Consulted the people doing the work before redesigning it, including frontline staff
- Tested or piloted a change rather than imposing it agency wide at once
- Checked that the change did not weaken safeguards such as incident reporting, documentation or supervision
- Reports the result with specifics, and mentions how the change was sustained or adjusted afterwards

questions.text: In this role, you'll collaborate with directors across Quality Assurance, Youth Services, HR, and Health & Safety. How would you foster alignment and break down silos between these areas?
questions.answerKey:
- Starts by learning each area's pressures and constraints before proposing shared processes
- Sets up regular cross functional forums with a clear purpose, and shared visibility of data such as incidents, training compliance and staffing
- Ties alignment back to a shared reference point: quality of support for people supported and the agency's obligations to MCFD and CLBC
- Handles conflict between areas directly rather than routing everything through the CEO
- Clarifies decision rights and handoffs so accountability is not lost between departments
- Gives an example of having actually reduced a silo, with what changed as a result

questions.text: Give us an example of when you successfully implemented operational changes that had a measurable impact on organizational performance
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a specific change with a clear before and after picture
- Names the measure used, for example turnover, vacancy rates, overtime, incident follow up times, or audit findings
- Explains how staff were prepared, trained and supported through the change
- Acknowledges resistance or unintended effects and how these were addressed
- Shows the improvement held over time, with a mechanism to monitor it

questions.text: How do you approach implementing new procedures, while still maintaining a strong company culture?
questions.answerKey:
- Explains the reason for a new procedure and how it connects to safety, quality or funder requirements, not just compliance
- Consults staff who will use the procedure and adjusts it based on what they raise
- Phases in change with training, clear written guidance and a named person to ask
- Watches for procedures that add burden without benefit and is willing to remove or simplify them
- Protects values such as person-centred practice and self-determination so process does not override responsiveness to people supported
- Follows up after implementation to check the procedure is workable in practice

questions.text: Describe your experience with financial planning and resource allocation. Can you share a time when you had to make difficult decisions to balance budget constraints with service delivery goals?
questions.answerKey:
- Concrete experience building or holding a budget, ideally with contract or grant funding such as MCFD or CLBC, including staffing costs, overtime and vacancy management
- A specific decision where funds were limited, showing what was protected and what was reduced, with direct support to people supported and staffing safety treated as the last thing to cut
- Reasoning that starts from impact on people supported and on frontline staff rather than from the spreadsheet alone
- Consulted program managers and finance before deciding, and was transparent with staff about what was changing and why
- Monitored the result afterwards and adjusted, rather than setting the budget and leaving it
- Awareness of funder reporting obligations and the limits on moving money between funded programs

questions.text: How do you use financial data and KPIs to guide operational decision-making?
questions.answerKey:
- Names the measures they actually watch, for example overtime and agency use, vacancy and turnover, occupancy or service utilisation, incident volume and trends, training compliance, variance to budget
- Uses trend over time rather than a single month, and checks the number against what managers are seeing on the ground before acting
- Gives an example of a number prompting a question and a conversation, not an automatic decision
- Balances financial indicators against quality and safety indicators, and can say what they would do if the two pulled in opposite directions
- Shares data back with program managers in a usable form so they can act on it, rather than holding it centrally

questions.text: What is your leadership style, and how have you adapted it in different organizational contexts?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a style in plain terms with evidence, not a label, for example how they run supervision, how decisions get made, how they handle disagreement
- Concrete example of flexing approach to context, for example more directive in a crisis or protocol situation, more collaborative in planning and program development
- Recognises the difference between leading experienced managers and supporting newer or single-staffed frontline teams
- Shows self awareness about their own regulation and default under pressure, and what they do to manage it
- Visible and accessible to frontline staff, understands the reality of residential and outreach work rather than leading only from the office
- Willing to name their own mistakes and what changed as a result

questions.text: Tell us about a time when you had to address underperformance at a senior or departmental level. What actions did you take and what was the result?
questions.answerKey:
- Named the concern directly and early with the person, with specific examples rather than general dissatisfaction
- Sought to understand contributing factors first, including workload, capacity, training gaps, or personal circumstances
- Set clear expectations, timelines and support, and documented the conversations and the plan
- Followed through, including escalating to formal performance management or ending the relationship where improvement did not happen
- Managed impact on the wider team and on continuity of service for people supported during the process
- Handled it respectfully and confidentially, and can describe the outcome honestly including if it did not resolve well

questions.text: This role requires representing the organization with external stakeholders and partners. Can you share a time when you built or strengthened key external relationships that benefited the organization?
questions.answerKey:
- Specific relationship named, for example a funder, school district, health service, housing provider or community organisation, and what it enabled
- Describes how trust was built over time: reliability, following through, being straight about problems rather than only presenting good news
- Concrete benefit to the organisation or to people supported, such as new referrals, a contract, shared resources or smoother transitions
- Handled a point of friction or a complaint from a partner without damaging the relationship
- Understands representing an agency means speaking within your mandate and knowing when to bring the board or executive in
- Awareness of confidentiality limits when discussing people supported with external partners

questions.text: What is your experience working with community members and stakeholders?
questions.answerKey:
- Direct experience with community groups, families, advocacy organisations, Indigenous partners, or neighbourhood consultation
- Examples of listening and adjusting plans based on what community members said, not just informing them
- Comfort with people supported and families as stakeholders with a voice in service design, consistent with self-determination
- Handled community concern or opposition, for example about a residential home in a neighbourhood, in a way that respected the privacy and dignity of people supported
- Sustained the relationship past the initial project rather than engaging only when something was needed

questions.text: What role has data-driven decision-making played in your past leadership positions? Can you give a specific example where data insights led to operational improvements?
questions.answerKey:
- A specific example with the actual data source named, for example incident reports, overtime records, turnover data, service utilisation or audit findings
- Describes what the data showed, what change was made, and how they knew it worked
- Combined the numbers with what staff and people supported reported, recognising the limits of data on its own
- Attentive to data quality, for example inconsistent incident reporting or gaps in documentation, and worked on that as part of the fix
- Careful with personal information: aggregated and de-identified where appropriate
- Willing to say when data disproved their own assumption

questions.text: What is your experience in the social service sector?
questions.answerKey:
- Relevant sector experience described concretely: populations served, service types such as residential, community inclusion, youth or employment services, and their own role
- Familiarity with contracted or funded service delivery and the accountability that comes with MCFD or CLBC style funding
- Understanding of core practice expectations: duty to report, incident reporting tiers, person-centred and trauma informed support
- Understands what frontline work actually involves, including single-staffed shifts, behaviour support, and staff exposure to critical incidents
- If coming from outside the sector, shows realistic understanding of the differences and how they would learn, without overstating what they know

questions.text: This position includes ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements, while managing operational risk. Tell us about a time when you had to follow regulations while also dealing with risks in day-to-day operations. How did you handle it, and what happened as a result?
questions.answerKey:
- Specific example involving licensing, accreditation, funder requirements, health and safety or employment standards
- Treated compliance as a floor for safety of people supported and staff, not as paperwork for its own sake
- Identified a real operational risk, assessed it, and took a proportionate action rather than either ignoring or over-reacting
- Escalated appropriately and reported externally where required, for example a reportable incident, duty to report, or notifying the funder or licensing
- Documented decisions and rationale, and made sure staff knew what changed and why
- Followed up with a review or debrief and adjusted practice so the risk was less likely to recur

questions.text: Why do you feel you are the right candidate to take on this high-level, cross-functional leadership role with Milieu?
questions.answerKey:
- Connects their own experience to the breadth of Milieu's work across adult and youth services and multiple geographic regions
- Demonstrates fit with the mission and values, particularly person-centred practice and self-determination, with an example rather than a restatement
- Evidence of working across functions, for example operations, finance, HR and program leadership, and holding competing priorities
- Honest about gaps and how they would address them in the first months
- Shows they have thought about how a senior operational role serves the frontline and the people supported, not just the organisation
- Realistic about the pace and pressure of the sector and how they sustain themselves in it

questions.text: Do you have any limitations that would prevent you from completing your job responsibilities?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can perform the core duties of the role, including travel across service regions and after hours availability if required
- Note any accommodation the candidate raises and follow up separately on what could be provided
- Confirm driver's licence, vehicle and any screening or clearance requirements the role carries
- Record the answer factually; do not probe into medical detail

questions.text: Do you have any plans to be away for any period of time, that we should be aware of?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm dates of any planned absence, booked travel or prior commitments
- Confirm earliest available start date and any notice period owed to a current employer
- Note anything affecting availability during onboarding or orientation and follow up on scheduling

questions.text: What do you know about our Agency?
questions.answerKey:
- Knows Milieu is a Surrey based multi-service agency operating since 1989, serving the Lower Mainland, Vancouver Island and Kelowna
- Names the two streams: adults with diversabilities from the start, children, youth and families added in 1999
- Can name concrete programs: residential homes, community inclusion, employment services, youth centre and learning centre, respite, outreach
- Aware funding comes largely from MCFD and CLBC, and of the alternative school partnership with the Vancouver School Board
- Speaks to the mission of supporting people as valued, contributing citizens, and to values such as respect, inclusiveness and self-determination
- Shows genuine preparation rather than reciting a website line, and connects what Milieu does to why they applied

questions.text: Tell us what you know about the Community living field (CLBC/MCFD)?
questions.answerKey:
- Distinguishes CLBC as the funder for adults with diversabilities and MCFD as the funder for children, youth and family services
- Understands the field supports people to live, work and participate in their own communities rather than in institutional settings
- Familiar with the language of person centred support, individual support plans and self-determination
- Aware that agencies in this field are contracted and accountable to their funders, which shapes hiring standards such as criminal record checks, references and training requirements
- Honest about the limits of their knowledge and shows willingness to learn the sector

questions.text: What interested you about the HR Assistant position at Milieu?
questions.answerKey:
- Interest in HR practice specifically, not just any office role: recruitment, onboarding, records, coordination
- Draws a connection between back office work and the quality of support people receive, for example getting the right staff hired and cleared quickly
- Some grounding for the non-profit or social services setting, whether lived, volunteer or work experience
- Realistic about the pace and volume of a high turnover, multi-site agency
- Names something concrete about Milieu rather than a generic statement about wanting to help people

questions.text: What do you think this job entails?
questions.answerKey:
- Full cycle recruitment support: posting jobs, screening resumes, scheduling and coordinating interviews, reference checks
- Pre-employment clearances and onboarding paperwork: criminal record checks, credentials, training records, new hire files
- Maintaining accurate personnel files and HR databases, tracking expiry dates and following up on missing items
- Acting as a first point of contact for managers and applicants, responding to routine enquiries and escalating anything sensitive
- Understands the work is largely administrative and detail driven, and that HR handles confidential information about staff and about people supported

questions.text: What do you consider your administrative strengths to be?
questions.answerKey:
- Names specific strengths with an example attached, not just adjectives: accuracy, tracking systems, file organisation, meeting deadlines
- Describes how they keep themselves organised, such as checklists, trackers, calendar reminders or tickler systems for follow-ups
- Comfort with high volume routine work and with interruptions
- Clear, professional written and phone communication with a range of people
- Discretion with confidential information and awareness of what can and cannot be shared

questions.text: What two words would your past supervisors use to describe you?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives two words and backs each with a concrete example or piece of feedback from that supervisor
- Words that fit the role, such as reliable, thorough, organised, calm, approachable
- Some self awareness rather than pure self-promotion, including how they responded to feedback
- Answer is consistent with what references would likely confirm

questions.text: Can you tell us about your experience with Microsoft Office, particularly Excel? Tell us how you have used these tools in your previous roles, and if you've worked with any other platforms or software relevant to your work
questions.answerKey:
- Specific Excel functions used, for example sorting and filtering, formulas, VLOOKUP or pivot tables, and what the spreadsheet was actually tracking
- Word and Outlook in practice: templates, mail merges, letters, high volume scheduling and email management
- Names any HRIS, payroll, applicant tracking or scheduling system used, and describes what they did in it
- Describes how they check their own work for errors in data entry
- Realistic self-assessment of skill level and willingness to learn new systems

questions.text: As an HR Assistant, you'll manage multiple stages of recruitment, which requires keen attention to detail and thorough follow-up. Can you share an example of a time when you had to be particularly meticulous in your documentation or follow-up to ensure a successful outcome?"
questions.answerKey:
- A real example with enough detail to judge: what the task was, what could have gone wrong, and what they did
- A concrete tracking method, such as a spreadsheet, checklist or reminder system for outstanding items
- Persistent, professional follow-up with people who did not respond the first time
- Catching or preventing an error, and being accountable when something was missed
- Understands why accuracy matters here: incomplete clearances or credentials can delay a hire or put people supported at risk

questions.text: In the role of HR Assistant, you'll often need to balance urgent hiring requests from multiple managers while maintaining the overall integrity of the department. How do you prioritize and manage competing demands to ensure both individual and organizational needs are met?"
questions.answerKey:
- Uses clear criteria to prioritise, such as vacancies affecting direct support coverage, expiring clearances, or hard deadlines
- Communicates proactively with managers about realistic timelines rather than agreeing to everything
- Keeps a visible list or tracker so nothing sits unattended while urgent items are handled
- Holds process integrity under pressure: does not skip reference or clearance steps because a manager needs someone on shift
- Escalates to their supervisor when demands genuinely conflict or a shortcut is being requested
- Gives an example of managing competing requests without damaging the working relationship

questions.text: Administrative Support involves considerable hands-on, repetitive, and clerical tasks. How would you stay motivated?
questions.answerKey:
- Honest acknowledgement that the work is repetitive, without dismissing it as unimportant
- Connects the routine tasks to a visible outcome, such as staff getting onboarded and homes being covered
- Practical self-management: batching similar tasks, setting small targets, taking breaks to keep accuracy up
- Looks for ways to improve or streamline a process rather than only enduring it
- Evidence from past roles of sustaining accuracy over long stretches of clerical work

questions.text: Tell me about a specific contribution you made to improve team performance?
questions.answerKey:
- A specific contribution with a before and after, not a general claim about being a team player
- Identifies what the problem or gap was and how they noticed it
- Describes how they raised it and brought others on board rather than working around them
- Names a measurable or observable result, such as faster turnaround, fewer errors, less duplication
- Credits colleagues appropriately and shows they can take direction as well as initiative

questions.text: We support individuals from varying backgrounds. Can you tell me about a how you have handled any challenges when dealing with diverse backgrounds?
questions.answerKey:
