- A real situation involving difference in culture, language, age, ability, faith or background, described respectfully
- Adjusted their own approach, for example plain language, an interpreter, more time, or a different communication channel
- Checked their assumptions and asked the person what they needed rather than deciding for them
- Shows awareness of their own bias and of the power they hold in an HR or gatekeeping role
- Knows when to ask a colleague or supervisor for guidance rather than guessing
- Frames diversity as normal practice at Milieu, including with applicants, staff and people supported

questions.text: Describe a time when you have been involved in a work crisis. What was the situation?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete example from their own work history, not a hypothetical, with enough detail to picture the setting and their actual role in it
- Situation is genuinely a crisis rather than routine busyness, for example an urgent staffing gap, a safety or privacy incident, a payroll or records error with real consequence, or an escalation from a program
- Is clear about what was theirs to handle and where the situation sat with a manager or another department
- Describes information handled sensitively where people supported, staff files or personal information were involved
- Names what the pressure felt like and how they stayed steady, rather than presenting themselves as unaffected

questions.text: How did you handle it?
questions.answerKey:
- Took clear first steps to stabilise the situation and worked out what was urgent versus what could wait
- Escalated to a manager promptly with the facts, rather than deciding alone or delaying to avoid looking uncertain
- Communicated with the people affected, staff, programs or external contacts, and kept them updated
- Kept a record of what happened and what was done, and followed the reporting process the workplace expected
- Managed their own regulation under pressure, stayed courteous with people who were upset, and asked for help when needed
- Respected confidentiality and shared information only with those who needed it

questions.text: What was the result?
questions.answerKey:
- States a specific outcome, including where it was partly unresolved, rather than only a positive summary
- Can say what the impact was on staff, programs or people supported
- Notes any follow up they carried out afterwards, such as corrected records, a debrief, or a check back with those involved
- Reflects honestly on what they would do differently and what they learned about their own limits
- Shows the outcome was reached with others, giving credit to the manager or team rather than claiming sole rescue

questions.text: Could it have been prevented?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a considered answer either way and explains the reasoning, rather than a reflexive yes or no
- Identifies a system or process cause, for example unclear handover, missing tracking, a gap in coverage, or information not passed on in time
- Takes appropriate personal responsibility without excessive self blame or blaming others
- Names a specific change that would reduce recurrence, such as a checklist, earlier escalation point, or better documentation
- Recognises some crises cannot be prevented and the useful work is in preparation and response

questions.text: Do you have any conditions, situations and/or pre-existing injuries that would impact your ability to do the job?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the candidate can perform the core duties of the role, including any sitting, computer work, lifting of files or supplies, and travel between sites
- Note any accommodation the candidate raises and record it for follow up with the hiring manager rather than exploring it further in the interview
- Keep the discussion to job requirements only, with no questions about diagnosis or medical history
- Follow up in writing on anything requiring assessment or an accommodation plan before start date

questions.text: Do you have any time off planned in the next 6 months?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm specific dates or approximate periods of planned absence in the next six months
- Confirm availability for the expected start date and any orientation or training days
- Note whether time off is already booked and non negotiable, such as travel already paid for
- Record the details to pass to the hiring manager for scheduling; no assessment of the answer itself

questions.text: What questions do you have for us?
questions.answerKey:
- Asks questions showing they have looked into the agency, its programs and the range of people supported
- Asks about the practical shape of the role, such as day to day duties, who they report to, training and orientation, and how the HR team works with programs
- Asks about expectations, supervision and how performance is reviewed
- Questions suggest interest in the work and the people served, not only pay and hours, though practical questions on schedule, pay and next steps are reasonable
- Confirms next steps in the hiring process, including references and criminal record check requirements

questions.text: What do you know about our agency?
questions.answerKey:
- Knows Milieu is a Surrey based social services agency operating since 1989, supporting adults with diversabilities and, since 1999, children, youth and families
- Aware services run across the Lower Mainland, Vancouver Island and Kelowna, and include residential homes, community inclusion, employment services and youth centres
- Understands maintenance work happens in people's homes and program sites, not empty buildings, and that funding comes largely from MCFD and CLBC
- Connects the mission of supporting people as valued, contributing citizens to keeping homes safe, clean and in good repair
- Has done some preparation rather than relying on general impressions of the sector

questions.text: What interests you about the role?
questions.answerKey:
- Genuine interest in hands on, varied work across multiple sites rather than a single fixed shop
- Comfort working around people supported and staff, and interest in a role where the work contributes to someone's home
- Realistic about the mix of scheduled upkeep, seasonal work and unplanned urgent repairs
- Values fit: respect for people's privacy and routines, patience, discretion
- Practical motivators are fine to state (stability, driving between sites, variety) as long as they are honest and specific

questions.text: How do you stay motivated?
questions.answerKey:
- Works from a task list or ticket system and gets satisfaction from closing out jobs properly
- Self directed when working alone at a site with little supervision
- Keeps standards up on routine or unglamorous tasks, not just the interesting repairs
- Notices and reports the impact of the work on people supported and staff as a source of motivation
- Names what they do when energy dips: reprioritise, check in with a supervisor, break large jobs into stages

questions.text: What are your strengths?
questions.answerKey:
- Names specific trade skills with evidence (plumbing, drywall, painting, minor electrical, appliance repair, grounds work) and is clear about limits
- Reliability and time management across several sites in a day
- Communication with house staff and managers about access, timing and what was done
- Awareness of boundaries and discretion around people supported and confidential information
- Safety mindset: WHMIS, ladders, tools, locking up, cleaning the work area

questions.text: How do you approach challenges?
questions.answerKey:
- Assesses the problem before acting, checks for hazards, and makes the area safe first
- Distinguishes what they can fix themselves from what needs a licensed trade or a quote, and escalates rather than working outside scope
- Communicates delays or access problems to the manager and staff at the site early
- Adapts when a home is occupied: reschedules noisy or disruptive work, works around routines of people supported
- Follows up to confirm the fix held and documents what was done

questions.text: How long have you worked in maintenance?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm number of years and the settings (residential, commercial, institutional, multi site)
- Confirm breadth of trades handled and any specialty
- Note any experience in occupied residential or care settings
- Follow up on gaps, recency, and whether the work was solo or supervised

questions.text: What qualifies you for this job?
questions.answerKey:
- Relevant trade or general maintenance background matched to the tasks in the posting
- Valid BC driver's licence and reliable ability to travel between sites, plus willingness to complete a criminal record check for work with vulnerable people
- Ability to work independently, prioritise urgent repairs and keep records of work completed
- Comfort and appropriate conduct in homes where people supported are present
- Any tickets or certifications relevant to the work (WHMIS, first aid, fall protection, gas or electrical limits)

questions.text: What type of training have you completed?
questions.answerKey:
- Formal trade training, apprenticeship or certificates, with the issuing body and currency
- Safety training: WHMIS, first aid, fall protection, lockout, asbestos awareness
- On the job training and any manufacturer or equipment specific training
- Openness to agency required orientation and training for working around people supported
- Confirm what is current versus expired and what would need renewal

questions.text: What were some of your previous responsibilities?
questions.answerKey:
- Concrete list of routine duties: preventive maintenance, repairs, painting, grounds, snow and seasonal work, appliance and fixture replacement
- Responding to urgent calls (leaks, heat, locks, floods) and prioritising them against scheduled work
- Coordinating with contractors, obtaining quotes, and being present for inspections
- Tracking work orders, keeping supplies and vehicle stocked, and recording completed jobs
- Any responsibility for keys, alarms, site access or building safety checks

questions.text: Do you have experience leading a team?
questions.answerKey:
- Clear account of scope: number of people, casual or formal supervision, contractors or staff
- Assigning and sequencing work, checking quality, and following up on incomplete jobs
- Handling a performance or safety issue directly and knowing when to bring it to a manager
- Honest if leadership experience is limited, with examples of mentoring, training a new worker or directing a contractor
- Willingness to work under direction as well as lead

questions.text: How would your previous employer describe you?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes themselves in terms an employer could verify: dependable, punctual, tidy, finishes what is started
- Gives an example that backs the description rather than adjectives alone
- Acknowledges a development area honestly without deflecting
- Comments on how they handled feedback or direction from a supervisor
- Names references who can speak to the work and is comfortable with them being contacted

questions.text: Can you describe a technical challenge you solved while on the job?
questions.answerKey:
- Specific problem with detail: what was failing, how they diagnosed it, what they ruled out
- Steps taken to make the site safe and limit disruption to people living or working there
- Knowing when to stop and bring in a licensed trade rather than improvising
- The outcome, cost or time considerations, and any preventive step taken afterwards
- Documented and reported the work to the manager or site staff

questions.text: Do you have any experience with HVAC systems?
questions.answerKey:
- States plainly what hands on HVAC work they have done: filter changes, belts, thermostats, condensate lines, seasonal furnace and rooftop unit checks
- Distinguishes what they can do themselves from what needs a ticketed gas or refrigeration contractor, and does not overstate
- Names any certification, ticket or formal training, and interviewer confirms the detail to follow up on
- Describes checking heating and cooling in homes before seasonal extremes rather than waiting for a complaint
- Notes working around people in their home: noise, access to bedrooms, timing the work so it disrupts the household as little as possible

questions.text: Do you have experience managing budgets and schedules?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete example of working to a materials budget, getting quotes, and flagging costs to a manager before spending rather than after
- Describes scheduling across multiple sites and juggling routine work against urgent calls
- Shows judgement about what is a genuine emergency (no heat, no hot water, unsafe door or lock, flooding) and what can wait
- Tracks purchases, receipts and work orders so a manager can see where money and time went
- Coordinates access dates with program staff rather than arriving unannounced at a home

questions.text: Can you describe your knowledge of maintenance standards?
questions.answerKey:
- Talks about the condition a residential home has to be kept in: working smoke and CO alarms, safe egress, hot water temperature, handrails, lighting, no trip hazards
- Mentions that homes are subject to licensing or funder inspection and that maintenance deficiencies get noticed there
- References WorkSafeBC requirements, WHMIS and safe storage of chemicals, tools and ladders away from people supported
- Understands accessibility needs: grab bars, ramps, door widths, equipment used by people with diversabilities
- Distinguishes cosmetic work from safety critical work and prioritises accordingly

questions.text: Describe your knowledge of preventative maintenance regulations
questions.answerKey:
- Describes a scheduled cycle of checks rather than reactive fixing: alarms, extinguishers, emergency lighting, furnace filters, gutters, water heaters, generator or sump if present
- Knows which items have mandated intervals and inspection tags, such as fire extinguishers and fire safety equipment
- Keeps a record per site so it is clear when each item was last serviced and when it is next due
- Mentions annual or seasonal servicing done by licensed trades and keeping their reports on file
- Connects preventative work to reducing disruption for the people living in the home

questions.text: What approaches do you take when inspecting electrical, plumbing and ventilation systems?
questions.answerKey:
- Works to a consistent checklist per system rather than only looking at what was reported
- Electrical: panel labelling, breaker condition, GFCI testing, outlet and cover plate condition, no overloaded circuits or damaged cords
- Plumbing: leaks under sinks, water temperature at taps, drainage, toilets, signs of moisture damage or mould
- Ventilation: filters, bath and range fans actually moving air, vents clear, dryer venting
- States clearly where they stop and call a licensed electrician, plumber or gas fitter
- Isolates or makes safe anything hazardous immediately, tells staff on shift, and reports it up rather than leaving it for the next visit

questions.text: How do you determine when it's more appropriate to replace a component or system rather than repair it?
questions.answerKey:
- Weighs repair cost and parts availability against remaining life and replacement cost
- Considers repeat failure history: a third or fourth service call on the same unit points to replacement
- Factors in safety and reliability, especially for heat, hot water, locks and anything a person supported depends on daily
- Recognises the decision is a recommendation, not theirs alone: brings options and costs to the manager to approve
- Considers downtime and impact on the household, including whether people would have to relocate during the work

questions.text: What methods do you use to ensure you're up-to-date on current regulatory standards?
questions.answerKey:
- Names actual sources: WorkSafeBC bulletins, BC building, electrical or plumbing code updates, municipal requirements, supplier and manufacturer information
- Keeps tickets and certifications current and does required refreshers
- Asks licensed trades and inspectors questions while they are on site
- Passes relevant changes on to managers when it affects how a home has to be maintained
- Admits when something is outside their scope and looks it up or asks rather than guessing

questions.text: How do you ensure the timely repairs of equipment or system components?
questions.answerKey:
- Has a single intake point for requests so nothing gets lost in texts or hallway conversations
- Triages by risk and impact on people supported, not by who asked most recently
- Keeps common parts and consumables stocked so routine fixes do not wait on ordering
- Communicates realistic timelines back to program staff and updates them when something slips
- Puts an interim safe measure in place when a full repair will take time, and confirms staff know about it
- Follows up to confirm the fix held rather than assuming it did

questions.text: What measures do you take to ensure that you comply with health and safety regulations while on the job?
questions.answerKey:
- Uses appropriate PPE, lockout of power or water, ladders and tools used as intended
- Secures the work area, tools, chemicals and small parts so people supported and children cannot access them
- Follows WHMIS and safe storage and labelling of products
- Tells staff on shift what they are doing, where, and for how long, and checks whether anyone in the home needs particular consideration before starting
- Reports incidents, injuries and near misses to a manager and completes the required incident documentation
- Stops work and escalates rather than proceeding with something unsafe or outside their ticket

questions.text: How do you ensure accurate documentation and record-keeping of maintenance tasks?
questions.answerKey:
- Records work at the time it is done, not from memory days later: date, site, what was found, what was done, parts used, time spent
- Notes outstanding deficiencies and follow up needed so the next person can pick it up
- Keeps contractor invoices, service reports and inspection tags filed by site
- Writes factually and without personal detail about the people living in the home
- Documentation is usable by others: a manager or licensing reviewer can see service history at a glance

questions.text: How do you ensure your work meets expectations?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirms scope and expectations with the manager or requester up front rather than assuming
- Inspects their own work before leaving and cleans the site so the home is left usable
- Checks back with staff at the home to confirm the issue is actually resolved
- Welcomes feedback and corrects work without defensiveness
- Consistent standard across sites regardless of who is watching

questions.text: How would you handle a maintenance issue you're unfamiliar with?
questions.answerKey:
- Says openly that they would not attempt something beyond their skill or ticket
- Makes the situation safe first: shut off power or water, isolate the area, tell staff on shift
- Researches or consults a colleague, supplier or licensed trade before proceeding
- Escalates to the manager with the problem, options and likely cost rather than going quiet
- Documents what was found and what interim measure is in place
- Treats it as a chance to learn so they can handle it next time

questions.text: What would you do if an accident occurs on the job?
questions.answerKey:
- Makes the area safe first: stops work, isolates the hazard (power, tools, spill, ladder), and moves people supported and staff away from the risk
- Attends to injury within their level of first aid training, calls 911 if needed, and does not leave an injured person alone
- Notifies the site supervisor or manager right away rather than handling it quietly, including when the injury seems minor
- Completes the incident documentation the same shift, with plain factual detail on what happened, and understands injuries to staff or a person supported follow the agency incident reporting process and WorkSafeBC requirements where applicable
- Preserves the scene or equipment where practical so the cause can be reviewed, and does not resume the task until it is cleared
- Follows up: reviews what led to it, flags the hazard so it is corrected for the next person, and reflects on their own state before returning to work

questions.text: Do you have any questions about the job?
questions.answerKey:
- Confirm the practical items the candidate raises: hours, on call or after hours expectations, travel between sites across the Lower Mainland, vehicle and driver's licence, tools supplied versus own tools
- Note any questions about working in homes where people supported live, including expectations around privacy, boundaries and giving notice before entering
- Record questions the interviewer cannot answer for follow up by the hiring manager
- Interest in scope of work, criminal record check, orientation and safety training is a reasonable sign of preparation; no questions is not on its own a concern

name: Victoria Staff Applicant
description: Applicants to the Victoria youth homes.

questions.text: What interested you to Milieu?
questions.answerKey:
- Has looked into Milieu beyond the job posting: multi service agency, youth residential and outreach, MCFD and CLBC funded work
- Connects the mission of supporting people as valued, contributing citizens in community to how they already work
- Names the population they want to work with (youth in residential care, youth in transition) and why, without romanticising the work
- Realistic about the demands: single staffed shifts, evenings and overnights, behaviour and crisis work
- Some sense of what they want to learn or build in this role, not just needing employment

questions.text: Tell the applicant about our youth home in general and the new homes in Victoria
The position may require you to provide outreach supports to youth. What do you think this would involve? Do you have experience with this, and would you be comfortable doing so?
questions.answerKey:
- Describes meeting a youth in the community rather than in a home: transport to appointments, school, family visits, life skills, recreation, check ins
- Understands the goals come from the youth's plan and support guidelines, and that the work is relationship based, not supervision only
- Names safety practice for community and lone work: knowing the plan, checking in with the on call or manager, phone charged, meeting in appropriate public settings, leaving if unsafe
- Comfortable with driving, and with unpredictability such as a youth not showing up or wanting to change plans
- Gives concrete prior experience with outreach, in home support, or community based youth work, or is honest about limited experience and what they would need
- Clear on boundaries in less supervised settings: no personal contact information, no personal vehicle use outside policy, documenting every contact

questions.text: How would you provide support if the child/youth have a history of trauma and attachment difficulties?
questions.answerKey:
- Prioritises predictability and consistency: routines, clear expectations, following through on what was promised, warning about changes ahead of time
- Reads behaviour as communication and a stress response rather than manipulation or defiance
- Builds relationship at the youth's pace, tolerates rejection and testing without withdrawing or taking it personally
- Offers choice and control in everyday moments so the youth is not repeatedly in a powerless position
- Works from the individual support plan and guidelines and shares observations with the team so the approach stays consistent across staff
- Attends to their own regulation, knowing a dysregulated adult escalates a dysregulated youth

questions.text: How do you assess and maintain your own safety while still being supportive to a child/youth in crisis?
questions.answerKey:
- Scans the environment before and during: exits, distance, positioning, objects that could be thrown, removing other youth from the area
- Uses an ongoing risk read along the lines of RADAR: recognise the change, assess, decide, act, review afterwards
- Keeps a calm voice and non threatening body language, gives space rather than crowding or blocking
- Knows the youth's safety and behaviour support plan and known triggers before the shift starts
- Calls for backup, on call or manager, or emergency services when the risk exceeds what one person can safely manage, and does not treat leaving the room as failure
- Names their own signs of activation and how they steady themselves, and debriefs and documents afterwards

questions.text: What is your experience and knowledge working with young people who use substances
questions.answerKey:
- Gives actual experience: youth using cannabis, alcohol, stimulants or opioids, and what they did in the moment
- Works from harm reduction rather than punishment or moral pressure: safer use information, not using alone, non judgemental conversation
- Knows overdose response, including recognising signs, calling 911, and administering Narcan or naloxone
- Keeps the relationship open so the youth will disclose, while still reporting and documenting as required and informing the manager or on call
- Understands substance use in the context of trauma, and does not make support or connection conditional on abstinence
- Knows the limits of their role and when to loop in the team, MCFD social worker, or specialised youth substance use services

questions.text: Children/youth we support sometimes have emotional outbursts that escalate into yelling and aggression. What strategies have you used to de-escalate a situation like this?
questions.answerKey:
- Notices early warning signs and intervenes before full escalation, using known triggers from the youth's plan
- Lowers stimulation: quieter voice, fewer words, reduced audience, more physical space, time rather than immediate demands
- Avoids power struggles: drops non essential demands, does not argue, correct or issue ultimatums mid escalation, offers limited real choices
- Validates the feeling while holding the safety limit, and stays with the youth if it is safe to do so
- Keeps everyone else safe: moves other youth away, clears hazards, calls for support or on call as needed
- Gives a specific example with a real outcome, including what they would do differently, and describes debrief and documentation afterwards

questions.text: What steps would you take immediately after a crisis to re-establish a supportive connection with the child/youth?
questions.answerKey:
- Allows recovery time first, offers water, food, quiet, presence without demanding conversation or apology
- Checks the youth for injury and checks on other youth in the home
- Approaches with warmth and no shaming, making clear the relationship is intact and the youth is not in trouble for having a hard time
- Revisits what happened only when the youth is regulated, curious about what triggered it and what would help next time
- Repairs their own part if they contributed, such as pushing a demand at the wrong moment
- Attends to their own regulation, debriefs with the team or manager, and completes the incident documentation accurately

questions.text: What would you do if the child/youth become physical with you, laying hands on you?
questions.answerKey:
- First response is to protect themselves and others by disengaging, creating distance, and removing other youth from the area
- Stays calm and does not retaliate, lecture or escalate; keeps voice and body language low key
- Uses Mandt trained blocking or release skills, with physical intervention only as a last resort where there is risk to life or limb
- Calls for support: second staff, on call or manager, and police or ambulance if the risk warrants it
- Reports and documents as a critical or reportable incident per the incident process, and notifies the manager promptly
- Recognises their own emotional reaction, seeks debrief, and returns to repair the relationship with the youth once both are settled

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to set a firm boundary with a child/youth and how they responded
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a concrete situation, the boundary set, and why it mattered for safety or fairness
- Set the limit calmly and briefly, with the reason, rather than as a threat or a punishment
- Held the limit consistently while staying connected and offering choice within it
- Describes the youth's reaction honestly, including anger, testing or withdrawal, and how they stayed steady through it
- Checked in and repaired afterwards, and passed the information to the team so the boundary held across shifts
- Reflects on whether the boundary was the right one and what they would adjust

questions.text: What does healthy boundaries mean to you when you're working with the children/youth?
questions.answerKey:
- Warm and caring, but a professional relationship, not friendship, parenting or rescuing
- Concrete practices: no personal phone number or social media, no personal contact outside shift, no gifts or money, no sharing personal problems with a youth
- Limited and purposeful self disclosure, used only when it serves the youth
- Consistency across staff so a youth cannot be caught between different rules, and no secrets kept from the team
- Recognises boundary drift in themselves, such as favouritism or feeling indispensable, and takes it to a supervisor
- Understands the power imbalance with vulnerable youth and the duty to report any concern about another person's conduct

questions.text: You will be trained in mandt upon hire and will get annual retraining. As an approved last resort and for life or limp situation, at times, staff will need to use the physical technique of the side body hug or similar, would be comfortable with doing the hold if trained and it is approved to do so?
questions.answerKey:
- Gives a clear yes or no about willingness to perform an approved hold once trained and certified
- Understands physical intervention is a last resort for risk to life or limb, after de-escalation options are exhausted
- Any prior training or hands on experience, and how that went for them
- Names any physical limitation, injury or personal factor the interviewer needs to follow up on
- Understands each use requires reporting and documentation as an incident, plus debrief with the youth and the team
- Note any hesitation or discomfort expressed, for follow up before hire

questions.text: You notice a child/youth hasn't showered or engaged in hygiene in several days and refuses when you suggest it. How would you support them?
questions.answerKey:
- Gets curious about what is behind the refusal rather than treating it as defiance: low mood, sensory issues, trauma history around bathrooms or being unclothed, lack of privacy, no products they like, depression or illness
- Avoids a power struggle or ultimatum; offers choice and control over timing, water temperature, music, products, whether staff are nearby or not
- Builds on relationship and routine, for example pairing hygiene with an activity, laying out clean clothes, normalising it without shaming or discussing it in front of peers
- Preserves dignity and privacy, including around gender, culture and body image, and keeps the conversation one to one
- Checks the person's ISP or individual support guidelines and asks the team what has worked before, so the approach is consistent
- Documents the pattern and raises it with the manager or team if it continues, since several days can signal a health or mental health concern needing follow up

questions.text: How would you handle a conflict with a coworker? What steps would you take to resolve it?
questions.answerKey:
- Goes directly to the coworker first, privately and respectfully, at a time away from people supported
- Separates the issue from the person: describes the specific behaviour or impact rather than character, and listens to the other side before deciding what happened
- Checks their own reaction and regulation first, and does not vent to other staff or in front of youth
- Escalates to the supervisor or manager if it cannot be resolved between them, if it affects the consistency of support, or if it involves a boundary, safety or practice concern
- Recognises the line where something stops being a conflict and becomes reportable, for example suspected abuse or neglect, and reports it regardless of the relationship
- Keeps working professionally with the coworker afterward and stays consistent for the people supported

questions.text: Most of the youth homes are single staffed, are you comfortable supporting youth one to one?
questions.answerKey:
- Clear yes or no on comfort with single staffed shifts, including overnights and weekends
- Shows realistic awareness of working alone: no immediate backup, decisions made in the moment, and reliance on the on call manager or supervisor by phone
- Describes how they stay safe and regulated alone, using de-escalation, giving space, positioning and exit awareness, and knowing when to call on call, crisis line or emergency services
- References relevant preparation or training, for example Mandt, RADAR, Narcan, safety plans and elopement response
- Gives an example of previous lone work or unsupported decision making, and how they documented and handed over afterward
- Interviewer to confirm any limits on shift types, locations or hours
